channel.title: Podcast — The world is too loud. Read what matters.
channel.description: Every day, the judgements worth remembering from 196 Chinese- and English-language podcasts. Points and quotes carry timestamps — tap one and you are back at the second it was said. Quotes are checked word for word and figures back to the source; anything unverifiable is cut, not published.

item.title: Germany's CDU Falls Out of a State Parliament: The Era of the Centre Is Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.description: The CDU won under 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz's authority is gone, and the populist far left and far right hold an overwhelming majority among voters under 35.
item.content:encoded:
The CDU won under 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz's authority is gone, and the populist far left and far right hold an overwhelming majority among voters under 35.

This is a piece of German domestic political commentary, not an interview. Information density is moderate, but it lays out the judgment that "populism has become the mainstream" very clearly — suited to anyone watching where European politics is heading.

0:00 The CDU is shut out of a state parliament for the first time
In the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state election, the CDU won under 5% of the vote and therefore holds no seats in that state parliament — the first time this has happened in the history of the Federal Republic. In the same election the AfD took roughly 38% of the vote, once again becoming the state's largest party. The author calls this the "final nail in the coffin" for Merz: he may cling to the chancellorship for a few more weeks or months, but his authority has vanished, his capacity to shape the country is completely exhausted — in political language, "a dead man walking."

0:00 The CDU's decline came later than the SPD's but is just as fatal
The CDU is the most important party in postwar German history, governing the Federal Republic for 53 of the past 77 years, and from Adenauer to Kohl to Merkel it left its mark on every aspect of the country. The author points out that in the early 2000s everyone was talking about "the crisis of social democracy," as the SPD fell from over 40% support to record lows; in hindsight, the fate of the centre-left big tent was merely a leading indicator of a broader crisis of the entire political centre, and the CDU subsequently walked the same road. The era of what Germans call the Volksparteien — catch-all parties capable of mobilising most of the vote — is effectively over.

0:00 Populists are not a fringe phenomenon but the most important political force
The author says this has been the most-asked question of the past decade: "Will the populist wave last, or is it about to peak?" In the summer of 2016, when Trump became the Republican nominee and Britain voted for Brexit, the answer seemed obvious to him; now the answer is undeniable — the populists are here to stay. What looked abnormal a few years ago has, whether you like it or not, become the mainstream. Populist politicians now hold power in the United States, India, Turkey and much of the democratic world, and have a high probability of taking office in France and Brazil in the coming months. Even where they remain in opposition, they are already strong enough to destroy any sense of business as usual.

0:00 The rise of one extremist party is feeding another
In the Berlin state election, Die Linke took 26% of the vote and emerged the big winner. The party descends from the SED, which ruled East Germany with an iron fist, and after reunification initially appealed mainly to older voters nostalgic for the security of the communist system; in recent years it has reinvented itself in the image of the global illiberal left, which the author considers roughly comparable to Zack Polanski's Greens in Britain or the more extreme parts of the DSA in the United States. During the campaign, some of the party's supporters were filmed chanting "Yalla, Yalla Intifada!"; on election night, the head of a notorious crime family visited the party's election party and cheerfully told the media he felt an affinity with it. The party's leader will very likely become the next mayor of Berlin — the first time an heir to the SED takes power in the capital.

0:00 Voters under 35 have swung to the two extremes
Another notable feature of the two elections is the age distribution. The SPD and CDU, which once dominated Germany's political landscape, now draw most of their support from pensioners. Among voters under 35, Die Linke and the AfD hold unassailable majorities in both Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. From this the author concludes that the tilt toward the extremes will only grow larger in the coming years. It also explains why the collapse of the centre is not a one-off election accident: the structure of the electorate itself is pushing the scales toward the two ends.

0:00 Mecklenburg-Vorpommern's left coalition is just an election accident
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, because a batch of other parties all failed to clear the 5% threshold for entering parliament, a broad left coalition just barely won enough votes to govern. But the author stresses that this is an election accident unlikely to repeat — a few thousand votes either way would leave the state completely ungovernable. The point is crucial: when centrist parties fall below the threshold, they don't just lose their own seats, they push the governability of the entire state to the edge of a cliff.

0:00 Don't surrender, and don't deny that the problem is real
The author explicitly rejects two responses. The first is to urge the centre to surrender: if the political middle can't hold, moderates might as well defect to the extremists on "their own side." He thinks this is wrong — neither Die Linke nor the AfD can solve the real problems Germany faces, and despite their vast differences they have conspicuous similarities, from their ambivalence toward Moscow to their persistent inability to purge antisemites from their own ranks. The second is to keep denying reality: for a decade the centre has attributed the extremists' success to foreign interference, social media algorithms, some candidate's tactical blunder, or the stupidity, sexism or racism of voters. The author says these ways of blinding yourself to the facts in front of you may be comforting, but they are just as dangerous.

item.title: Going overseas: don't wait until you're big to go to Europe and America — go there first to get big
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.description: Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and America once they're big, but it's exactly the reverse — you go there to become big. Get the region choice wrong and the later product 3.0 and channel pyramid won't stand up.
item.content:encoded:
Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and America once they're big, but it's exactly the reverse — you go there to become big. Get the region choice wrong and the later product 3.0 and channel pyramid won't stand up.

Wei Zhe compresses ten years of overseas investment experience into four choices, counterintuitive but each backed by cases and numbers, and the second half on AI transforming organisations and pricing is the most information-dense.

1:30 The old cross-border mega-seller path is a dead end
Wei Zhe says the ‘cross-border mega-seller’ popular in Shenzhen is a distribution-style mindset, with dozens or hundreds of accounts; he has seen companies with over a thousand accounts and hundreds of thousands of SKUs. Ten years ago these companies made money faster than other paths, and many investors liked them. But a distribution-style company is essentially a traffic-style company: the more stores, the more likely to get traffic. When platform goods aren't plentiful enough, distribution isn't opposed; once goods are plentiful enough, using distribution to grab traffic is bad money driving out good. More critically, three red lines: goods not matching descriptions harms consumers, brushing orders harms other merchants, and putting in little cards to build private domains harms the platform. Amazon's flywheel places great importance on consumer experience, and these behaviours hit exactly that protective wall.

4:38 Of the four choices, region comes first
Wei Zhe says it's not just cross-border e-commerce; all of life is about choices being more important than effort. He gives four choices: region choice, channel choice, product category choice, brand positioning choice. On region choice he has always advocated seizing the European and American markets first, because of strong paying power, high internet penetration, and more importantly the brand can build momentum. This isn't something they invented; when Japanese and Korean brands went global back then, they all seized Europe and America. On category choice they change their advice every three years: the earliest three years supported products common to China and abroad, where the domestic supply chain could sell overseas without modification, like Anker's power banks which were almost identical except for voltage; the second three years they advised overseas-exclusive products, because China's supply chain had all gone overseas and common products had no differentiation; the most recent three years is product 3.0 — electric, with chips, with algorithms.

12:29 It's not that you go to Europe and America after getting big, it's that you go there to get big
Many companies tell Wei Zhe ‘I'll go to Europe and America when I'm big’, and he says it's exactly the reverse — you go to Europe and America to get big. He gives the example of Cupshe, a swimwear company: a husband and wife, stocked $50,000 of goods, and their first stop was the US. $50,000 is goods for sale, actually very little, so there's no minimum threshold. He recently looked at AI smart hardware, starting from Kickstarter crowdfunding with a thousand or ten thousand products, even taking pre-orders before placing orders, with no capital — this is also a great way to test the waters. He even advises big companies entering the European and American markets to learn from small startups. They always say the needle must be fine enough to pierce in, and both big and small companies should first do the four singles well: single market, single category, single channel, single brand.

20:36 After AI, good companies don't just find demand, they create it
Wei Zhe says with AI, excellent companies don't go looking for demand, they should lead demand and create demand. He gives the example of a Chinese company making astronomical telescopes: originally not electric, they electrified it, with chips and algorithms; the algorithm is actually very simple, with GPS positioning, and the map of the universe's movements is regular. He wasn't an astronomy enthusiast but would buy one, click once at home in Silicon Valley, it automatically aligns Orion for you, tells you 3 a.m. is the best time, you press it and go to sleep, and the next day it has taken the photos for you. This lets everyone become a good astronomy enthusiast. Another example is a cross-border class student doing curtains: after electrifying them they didn't sell well in the US because American electricians are expensive, so he put solar panels on the windows, turning electric curtains that needed an electrician into DIY ones; originally always one or two hundred million, now four or five hundred million, with profit of one or two hundred million.

24:48 In the AI era, still using subscription fees means you're behind
Wei Zhe says in the AI era, if you still have the subscription-fee mindset you're behind again; they are all advising companies to do back-end charging, software charging, called tokenized. A monthly subscription fee is the dumbest way, a bit like advertising charging by time rather than by usage. This time AI has brought out the most ideal charging model in all of human education: paying according to your usage of AI software, services or content. He gives an example: Bessie, if you take two weeks off this month, isn't subscribing for a month wasting two weeks? They advise that AI-transformed hardware should be charged like AI, not going back to the old SaaS monthly $9.9 subscription model. An AI reading platform he looked at charges by how many articles you read, and doesn't charge if you don't read; the same with smart bike trainers, after topping up it's $1 per ride, $2 for two hours.

27:28 Adding AI is more worth favouring than AI plus
Wei Zhe has a view called AI plus or plus AI; he reverses the phrase and favours plus AI rather than today favouring AI plus. The difference is: plus AI is hardware humans have already accepted, which you AI-ify; rather than creating a hardware never seen before because of AI. It's very hard for humans to accept a completely new hardware. For example, Oura makes rings, because you first accepted rings; some things that hang a camera under your neck are harder for me, I haven't accepted that hardware. So they are very bullish on adding AI to already-accepted hardware. They invested in a capacitive stylus that is number one globally, because everyone already writes on a Pad, it doesn't add an extra pen for you, it just AI-ifies your pen. He also especially wants to transform one of the top one or two overseas fitness equipment companies, replacing the fitness coach on the screen with AI-generated ones — you want a man, it's a man, you want a black person, it's a black person, and with two cameras it can guide your workout with AI.

29:43 Channels aren't flat, they're a pyramid
Wei Zhe says channels aren't multiple channels multiple paths, each channel parallel or even competing; excellent brands all have a channel pyramid. Like luxury brands and traditional brands, there must be different channel strategies, pricing strategies, and which channel new products launch in first all have their rules. What is a light-goods channel, what is the main waist volume channel, the pyramid design differs for different categories and brands. He gives Anker: making power bank mecha seems a bit low, to enter the consumer electronics high ground of Soundcore earphones you have to get into Apple flagship stores; whether it really sells a lot isn't important, but it can transform the brand, Apple is the pyramid's tip. Pop Mart must open on London's Oxford Street, even if it doesn't make money how much can it lose, but it must hold up there. He says some companies treat Temu and AliExpress as parallel channels for selling goods, which definitely won't work; AliExpress is a light-goods channel, when Amazon delists you, dump it in that channel, you can't sell on Amazon and here too, consumers get confused.

36:14 R&D is 1, marketing is 0
Wei Zhe says he really dislikes splashing out on marketing expenses. Many Chinese brands going overseas or cross-border e-commerce are very willing to add 2% of revenue to marketing expenses, but consumers don't get it. He says do you dare add 2% of revenue to R&D expenses. He has met many bosses at the 1 billion or 2 billion scale; at 1 billion they say 20 million for R&D, I don't know what for. He says see, there's the problem, you don't know what for. Your 2% thrown at marketing expenses makes the platform happy, consumers don't get it; but 2% thrown into R&D consumers get it. He has always firmly believed good products speak for themselves, marketing is just, your R&D is 1, marketing is 0, if you have something good you can amplify it, if you don't have that 1 never put many 0s. He gives three judgment signals: first, dare to find a benchmark company, definitely a mid-to-upper brand, and you crush it by doubling performance; second, you sell at the same price as it; third, you sell online and hit offline channels to come to you.

item.title: The AI office hype hasn't cleared, and the personal Agent war has already begun | Breaking down Town, Instinct, Grok Bot and Muse
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-luanfanshu-10万用户估值100亿-个人agent的估值跑在产品前面/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-luanfanshu-10万用户估值100亿-个人agent的估值跑在产品前面/
item.description: Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't even officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal Agent heat, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.
item.content:encoded:
Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't even officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal Agent heat, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.

Four frontline product people break down the four paths of Town, Instinct, Grok Bot and Muse, and also explain why that batch of products like Xiaolongxia became martyrs. Information density is high, but the second half is worth more.

0:00 100,000 users prop up a $10 billion valuation
Instinct only began small-scale invite testing in February this year, and by the end of August it still hadn't reached 100,000 users, yet its valuation rose from $50 million at the start of the year to $500 million in August, then $2.5 billion at the end of August, and this month the new round being quoted in the market has already reached $10 billion, with Sequoia and Benchmark both in talks to lead. The founder is a 23-year-old unknown with no big-company experience, no technical patents, no industry background. Pan Luan (潘乱) put it bluntly: what capital is buying is neither the founder nor the product, it's the story of the next OpenAI, and it can pay the price of the next-generation personal operating system to grab a ticket.

15:16 The line between tool and person is initiative
The biggest difference between this wave of Agents and the last is that it is no longer another tool, but a person. Two differences between a person and a tool: first, long-term understanding — a tool needs the context explained again every time, while a person understands what kind of person you are like a friend or colleague; second, initiative — setting up an automated task in Manus still depends on prompts, on you spelling out the rules and intent, and that isn't initiative. True initiative is subjective agency — like the colleague who understands your goal in doing something and proactively comes over to say, "I have a plan, should we discuss it?"

18:09 Office Agents organise by project, personal Agents organise by person
The most core difference is the dimension along which context is built. Cloud Code builds context along a mission or project dimension, and switching to the next project means starting over; this wave of personal agents builds context centred on you as a person, knowing your profile, preferences and past history. Open Codex or Manus and the list on the left is all the tasks and projects you've sent out; open Grok Bot and beside it are AI companions you can drive together. Personal scenarios care less about model capability and the harness layer, because individuals don't have that many complex tasks, while office Agents care a lot about task completion rate.

30:28 Town first trades email for the user's right to delegate
The four products are trying to solve the same problem, just with different approaches. Town has a mobile client, but 70% of its data traffic is on PC, and it focuses on the email scenario, solving one high-frequency scenario well before expanding. It understands which emails you send and receive often, auto-archives, learns your writing style, drafts replies for you, and sends automatically after you click confirm. The email scenario is done more deeply than any other agent, and overseas it has already achieved fairly viral spread, especially in school-type scenarios. In one sentence: use a high-frequency scenario to build user trust, and acquire the user's ultimate right to delegate bit by bit.

39:33 Poke didn't break out, and it wasn't a technical limit
Poke and Instinct are both agents that live inside IM and don't make a standalone app, but Poke didn't break out. Suki believes it wasn't a technical limit — Browser Use was already very mature by the end of last year, and Poke could absolutely have done it at the time; the difference was team strategy: Instinct went deeper in the agent direction, taking the full-delegation route, able to access credit cards, screen and microphone, booking flights and buying things for you, things users had never seen, which produced viral spread; Poke put its energy into content push accuracy, taking the proactive-push route, with email notifications arriving even earlier than the inbox itself, but it didn't take the step of "finishing the thing for you".

42:39 Cloud Agents have to handle three environments
Mark says doing cloud agents was a painful lesson: a local agent and a cloud agent are completely different things. To do personal AI you have to be usable anytime, anywhere, and you can't be unreachable just because the computer screen is off. The cloud has to handle three environments — the user's device, the cloud service, and the agent's execution environment — and task state, task interruption and recovery, and context passing between the three environments are all very complex systems. They started in February, and just getting the agent to run stably on the cloud took at least two months; setting aside detours, polishing a sincere piece of work takes at least three to four months.

50:39 Hiring an assistant and being a middleman are two businesses
Town started out doing corporate tax filing, and after pivoting it leans more toward enterprise scenarios, with a relationship more like you paying for a personal assistant, naturally filtering for people willing to pay, with a typical profile of white-collar workers who are extremely busy and have no time or energy. Muse is more like a middleman, shopping guide or broker; although it has a paid subscription, the main projected revenue source is still commission from matchmaking transactions, leaning toward mass users and blending into everyday WhatsApp chats. Two completely different logics, and the scenarios they cut into and the users they filter out are different too.

1:14:07 For an Agent, the saved folder may be noise
The story Zuckerberg told when launching Muse was extracting what you like to eat from Instagram-saved ingredients, generating a shopping list, adjusting the menu by dinner party size and dietary restrictions, then completing the shopping and relationship maintenance — turning years of interest profile into money, going from a discovery platform to a decision-and-transaction platform. But Suki suspects this is to save face for the free business narrative: helping users close transactions is absolutely not among the top scenarios users want to solve; users more want to solve the annoying things they don't want to do themselves. There isn't that much high-quality context in the saved folder; truly high-quality context comes more from offline, IM and email, and Douyin and Instagram saves may themselves be noise to an agent.

item.title: Ten Years of Parenting Taught Me: When Your Kid Won't Listen, the Problem Isn't Your Kid
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-parentmojo-育儿十年才懂-孩子不听话时-问题不在孩子身上/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-parentmojo-育儿十年才懂-孩子不听话时-问题不在孩子身上/
item.description: On the podcast's tenth anniversary, the host revisits ten parenting beliefs she once held as certain — from forcing her daughter to take medicine to treating an expert's framework as truth. Each one she learned first in a book, then relearned in a real conflict.
item.content:encoded:
On the podcast's tenth anniversary, the host revisits ten parenting beliefs she once held as certain — from forcing her daughter to take medicine to treating an expert's framework as truth. Each one she learned first in a book, then relearned in a real conflict.

For parents who want to interrogate their own parenting methodology. Medium information density, heavy on personal narrative, but the ten reflections are clearly structured, and the back half — on the "village" and on the couple relationship — is more valuable than the front half.

6:00 Forcing the medicine won the behavior and lost the relationship
The host recalls her three-year-old daughter refusing antibiotics; she held her down and forced the medicine in, and her daughter threw most of it back up. That night her husband Alvin stayed with their daughter in the bathroom for an hour, calmly saying the whole time, "I'm willing to do anything, but we're not leaving until we figure this out." In the end the daughter finished the whole course herself, with small sips of medicine, small sips of water, and a small piece of chocolate to take the taste away. The host says the difference wasn't that her husband was more patient — it's that he wasn't solving a behavior, he was understanding what would actually help the child do this thing. What the child needed was autonomy over the process, and to feel she was on the same team as her parent rather than being held down to do something.

9:19 The authoritative parenting framework rests on 146 white kids
The host says she accepted uncritically early on that "authoritative is the best parenting style," because every blog and every study said so. It wasn't until she made the episode on corporal punishment that she found a paper co-authored by Diana Baumrind defending parents' ability to spank their children, and started digging. She found that this framework — cited more than 26,000 times, and defining sixty years of parenting research — was originally based on just 146 white, middle-class preschoolers in the town where Baumrind lived. She calls this evidence of her own insufficient critical thinking, and says she now asks at the macro level, "Does this theory make sense?" and at the micro level, "Does it fit this specific child in front of me?"

17:41 Not punishing your kid doesn't mean being ruled by your kid
The host says she once believed that without punishments and consequences a child would run wild — she even remembers standing in the shower when her daughter was four months old thinking, "How do I discipline her without becoming a mean mom?" Clinical psychologist Dr. Houri Parsi admitted in the membership community that she too had treated "obedience" as the goal, and that every tooth-brushing session was a battle. Once, recording for the host to watch, she deliberately withheld threats, punishments and rewards and simply asked her two-year-old son, "Why don't you want to brush your teeth?" He couldn't put it into words — he just called out "Mama" and buried his head in her chest. She realized what he wanted was time alone with her. She put the toilet lid down, sat down, held her son, and they sang a song together, and he brushed his own teeth — the whole thing took under five minutes.

21:31 "I need you to take out the trash" is not a need
The host says that looking back, she didn't understand what a "need" was — she thought saying "I need you to take out the trash" to her husband was a perfectly logical sentence. Before their daughter was born the two of them almost never argued: mountain biking in summer, skiing in winter, because the ad agency they worked at represented resorts and paid them in vouchers. Everything changed after their daughter was born: during his three weeks of paternity leave her husband would fetch her anything she wanted, and the rest of the time he was training for a hundred-mile ride and watching the Tour de France. She says it was learning that she had needs for "collaboration, partnership, and having her effort seen" that actually pried open the problems between them; before that she was carrying a large amount of resentment inside her with no idea how to handle it.

24:01 When you're triggered, the problem isn't the person who interrupted you
The host says her biggest trigger is being interrupted — the moment her husband interrupts her she flies into a rage, most recently over how much postage a package needed. She always assumed the cause was simply that her husband interrupted her, and that if he stopped, everything would be fine. Recording in July 2018 with intergenerational trauma expert Dr. Rebecca Babcock-Fenerci, she traced it live to her own father, a special education teacher who treated sixteen-year-olds like ten-year-olds and for a stretch lectured her every night. Later, in the car, she interrupted her daughter, and her daughter said, "Don't interrupt me, Mama," and her husband looked at her and said, "She's you." She says that was the moment she realized it had never been only about the two people in the room, and out of it she developed the "Tame Your Triggers" course, which grew from a one-month module to ten weeks.

30:27 The handmade book she made while pregnant was full of expectations for her child
The host describes a book she made while pregnant: three covers, one in the middle and one on each side, opening in both directions, brown book cloth with a beige spine, the word "me" cut out of the board on one cover and "you" embossed on the other when you flipped it over — the concept being "you came out of me." On the "me" side she wrote her own feelings and thoughts; on the "you" side she wrote to Carys, whom she had not yet met. She reads out the earliest batch of "expectations for you": I hope you're smart, or at least average; I hope you're the kind of kid who shakes hands with people instead of hiding behind my legs; I hope you like both roughhousing and pretty things; I hope you don't cry all the time; I hope when you fall you pick yourself up and say "I'm okay." She says looking back, her biggest mistake was not knowing how to simply be with a person, allowing them to be their whole self and witnessing that, without carrying ideas about how they should be.

33:14 Kohn's principle two: reconsider your demands first
The host says she once assumed she'd play the role of "enforcer" — she even wrote "I hope you can love me the way I love him" on her pregnancy expectations list. She says RIE loosened the soil for her, but what actually planted the seed was Alfie Kohn's Unconditional Parenting. She shares a few of its principles: principle two is to reconsider your demands — "maybe when a child won't do what you ask, the problem isn't the child, it's what you're asking"; principle five is to change how you look, not just how you act — when you see your child doing something you asked them not to do, your first reaction is curiosity about what they're struggling with, not how to make them stop; principle ten is to "attribute to your child the best motive consistent with the observed facts," and she says when she quotes it she changes the ending to "consistent with the observed behavior," because "there are no facts, only what we observe."

39:07 The couple relationship isn't a different subject, it's the same one
The host says she long believed the couple relationship and the parent-child relationship were completely different things — when she started the parenting membership eight years ago she asked Dr. Laura Froyen to write the co-parenting module, because she had no idea how to handle a partner relationship. She says her shift toward collaborative parenting was relatively easy, because she had no ten-year-old habits with her daughter; but she and Alvin had been together ten years without ever learning how to disagree, because they spent most of it doing hobbies they loved, and she didn't mind doing most of the housework. It wasn't until she did Gottman training that she realized this was almost the same work she'd been doing with her child all these years — while also believing the Gottman method itself has a few key flaws. She recruited couples from the membership to record real arguments, using modified tools, and one couple — where the husband had refused to discuss a toxic issue — became willing to talk after his wife listened for ten minutes with a genuine intent to understand him, and in that same session they reached an agreement to move forward.

item.title: NPR's comment section was mistaken for bots — it was actually a group of middle schoolers
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-tal-npr-评论区被当成机器人-其实是一群初中生/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-tal-npr-评论区被当成机器人-其实是一群初中生/
item.description: NPR staff saw gibberish flooding a comment section and reported it as bots; a younger colleague recognized it as kids whose parents had blocked social media, using a Spotify comment section as a group chat.
item.content:encoded:
NPR staff saw gibberish flooding a comment section and reported it as bots; a younger colleague recognized it as kids whose parents had blocked social media, using a Spotify comment section as a group chat.

Four independent stories, medium information density, but the generational misread in the first story and the mother-daughter conversation about braiding in the third are both worth hearing.

1:01 The gibberish comments aren't bots, they're kids
Dave Blanchard saw a sudden flood of incomprehensible messages in the Wild Card comment section on Spotify, assumed bots, and reported them to Spotify to be deleted. But Hannah Chin, a colleague at NPR ten years younger, opened the screenshots and immediately reached the opposite conclusion: these are children. Her evidence was the display names full of emoji that require a special character generator to type, the unfamiliar cartoon avatars, and the speech pattern of short back-and-forth lines with lots of exclamation points. Dave wasn't buying it at first, replying, "That's an interesting theory."

6:05 Using playlists as the group-chat entrance
Hannah kept digging and found how the kids operated: one child creates a public playlist called Let's Chat Here or New Chat containing just one podcast episode; other kids see the playlist, click into that episode, and chat in the comments. They also post Google Forms as quizzes, writing "only cool people can fill this out." Hannah said bots don't go post Google Forms, but Gen Alpha does, the way her own generation made UQuiz or BuzzFeed personality quizzes. That was the detail that convinced Dave.

8:06 They picked NPR because the comment section was empty
The show reached out to several commenters, and only one, a 14-year-old girl named Ella, agreed to be interviewed, speaking from the car while her father drove. Ella said the core group is about 20 kids, many in drama club, mostly girls, with strict parents who don't let them use regular social media. They first chatted in the comment section of a podcast that played TikTok videos; after that podcast got shut down, the kids started relocating via playlists. Asked why they chose NPR shows, Ella said: we look for podcasts with small comment sections, so we don't get pulled into other people's comments.

11:08 Dave needed a generational translator
After learning the truth, Dave said he felt guilty for having reported them, and also felt old. He said, "I literally needed Hannah to be my generational translator," and that this made him acutely aware of his age and how out of date he was. Ella said she's sure that one day she too will be as completely lost as Dave. The show puts this segment at the top, as the entry point to the episode's theme of "intergenerational space travel."

25:35 The wedding toast was a poem nobody understood
At 18, Courtney read a poem she wrote at her mother's second wedding, and her mother held it against her for thirty years. The poem opens with the mother walking in habitual darkness, every breath like her last; the middle describes the mother smoking by the counter; but the ending turns to "you found roots, you found a soul worth worshipping." The mother said that on the wedding day she only heard the negative first half and never heard the kindness at the end; rereading it, Courtney conceded that presenting a bride with such a dark picture on her wedding day would indeed make it hard to hear the good part.

31:52 The body knew the marriage was wrong first
Two days after the wedding, the 49-year-old mother suffered a massive stroke. Courtney offers a theory: the mother's body, not her mind, had known all along that the marriage was a mistake. The mother agreed, saying she knew when she bought the wedding dress, that she wasn't all that happy then, that she "anticipated this awfulness ahead of time," sensing it in every fiber. This exchange turns all the earlier arguing about the wedding toast into a question of why her mother didn't listen to her intuition back then.

39:05 Only throwing out the stepfather repaired the mother-daughter bond
Last October, the mother fell in the kitchen Mr. X designed and broke her back; Mr. X was too drunk to help and only handed her the phone hours later so she could call an ambulance herself. The mother was hospitalized for months and gave Courtney power of attorney to go to court and have Mr. X removed. Courtney said it was the hardest thing she's ever done, but they won. The mother said it was precisely because Courtney spent so much time here for that that she realized how much her daughter cared about her. Mr. X drove them apart; throwing him out pulled them back together.

55:41 The mother says braiding shouldn't be the entry to toughness
Myra Flynn locks horns with her six-year-old daughter Avalon every morning over braiding, and she blurted out "sometimes what we need isn't comfortable," then realized those were her own mother's words. She called her mother, Martha Mathis, expecting support, but her mother said: braiding shouldn't be the entry point for making a child tough, because it carries too many racial and gender meanings; and at six, Avalon is already the toughest little girl there is. Her mother's advice was to let Avalon handle a small section of hair herself, because "she'll be gentle with herself."

item.title: Intel's Optane Died Because 3D NAND Was Too Cheap, Not Because the Tech Failed
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-asianometry-intel-的-optane-死于-3d-nand-太便宜-不是技术不行/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-asianometry-intel-的-optane-死于-3d-nand-太便宜-不是技术不行/
item.description: Phase-change memory went from 1970 to 2022, and every time it was squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.
item.content:encoded:
Phase-change memory went from 1970 to 2022, and every time it was squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.

A complete history of a storage technology's failure, from RMM in 1970 to the shutdown of Optane in 2022. Information density is moderate; the second half, on data-center deployment and Micron's exit, is the most valuable part.

3:07 The physics of phase-change memory makes it slow
Phase-change memory stores data by switching a material between crystalline and amorphous states: the crystalline state has low resistance, the amorphous state high resistance, and the two differ by three to four orders of magnitude. Melting the material and quenching it into the amorphous state is called RESET; the reverse is called SET. SET either melts the material into a liquid and then cools it slowly to crystallize, or heats it to a temperature high enough to convert it directly to crystal without melting. The author points out that SET is often the speed bottleneck for PCM. This physical mechanism has not changed since Stanford Ovshinsky discovered the phase-change behavior of chalcogenide compounds in the 1960s.

4:13 Intel built phase-change memory in 1970, then forgot
In 1970, RG Neale and DL Nelson of Energy Conversion Devices and Gordon Moore of Intel published an article in Electronics magazine announcing "Read-Mostly Memory," positioned between RAM and ROM, for storing data that programs read often but rarely change. Each cell had a silicon diode plus a layer of phase-change material; Intel supplied the silicon substrate, ECD supplied the material. But in 1970 the minimum feature size was only 10 micrometers, power consumption was high, SET took milliseconds, and endurance was low. DRAM capacity was growing, EPROM arrived, and RMM disappeared. Years later, when someone asked the 79-year-old Moore about the article, he said he had no memory of it at all.

9:25 Numonyx treated PCM as its only shot at a comeback
The rise of NAND sent NOR flash into long-term decline, and in 2007 global NOR sales fell 9% year over year. Intel merged its NOR business with STMicroelectronics' flash business, forming the Swiss company Numonyx in 2008, with investment from Francisco Partners and bank loans. NOR lacked NAND's growth prospects, so Numonyx could only bet on PCM—PCM combined NOR's fast random reads with NAND's high-capacity storage, and in theory could replace both. In February 2008 Intel announced delivery of its first PCM prototype, Alverstone, at 128 megabits and 90 nanometers.

13:33 Mobile PCM was wiped out by a wave of 3D NAND
PCM's entry strategy was to attack the mobile market, replacing the NOR flash that stored boot code while also storing data. In 2009 Samsung announced a 512-megabit PRAM at 60 nanometers, saying that paired with DRAM it could save more than 20% in power. Micron acquired Numonyx in 2010 for about $1.2 billion in stock, and in July 2012 finally shipped 1-gigabit PCM at 45 nanometers, which Nokia put into its Asha feature phones. But in August 2013 Samsung announced mass production of 24-layer 3D NAND, and 3D NAND then set off the steepest cost-decline curve in semiconductor history, removing mobile PCM's most compelling rationale. In January 2014 Micron announced it was withdrawing from mobile PCM.

17:38 Intel and Micron were split from the start on Optane's positioning
In July 2018 Intel and Micron agreed to a friendly split, each going independent after completing joint development of the second generation of 3D XPoint. The disagreement was over product direction: Intel initially aimed Optane SSDs at consumer PCs and laptops, hoping to spread wafer costs through volume; Micron wanted to go straight into the data center. Jon Carter hinted in 2016 that consumer systems did not really need 3D XPoint's low latency, non-volatility and endurance, or at least not enough to pay four to five times the price of NAND. In October 2018 Micron announced it would pay $1.5 billion to buy Intel's half of the IM Flash plant in Utah, and Intel shifted to producing it itself.

22:47 Putting Optane in the data center required redoing motherboards and software
In April 2019 the first DIMM-form-factor Optane DC Persistent Memory went on sale, four years after 3D XPoint was announced, and it required matching Xeon processors, chipsets and motherboards. It had two modes: Memory Mode combined Optane and DRAM into one volatile memory pool, worked out of the box, but its value depended on DRAM price fluctuations; App Direct Mode was the truly valuable mode, letting software write persistent data to Optane so it survived a reboot. Oracle or SAP databases typically take more than an hour to reload data from SSDs or hard drives after a restart, and Optane could eliminate that. One imprecise but directional test showed a 12.5x improvement. But App Direct Mode required programmers to rethink data consistency issues.

24:51 Only 40% of 582 proofs of concept used the truly useful mode
In 2020 Intel updated Optane adoption, saying there were 582 proofs of concept in the pipeline, with SAP HANA and Oracle Exadata as the main users and the rest mostly in high-performance computing, infrastructure and some AI analytics. But only 40% used the more valuable App Direct Mode. Intel said it believed the industry would eventually adopt that mode, but it might take years. In the same period Intel announced the sale of its 3D NAND business to SK hynix for $9 billion, with Optane not included in the deal, which looked like an endorsement but also let people infer that Optane's implied loss in 2020 exceeded $500 million.

25:52 After Micron's exit, Optane was left with a single supplier
In March 2021 Micron announced it was immediately stopping 3D XPoint development, saying the Utah plant had long suffered from underutilization and dragged the company down by $400 million a year; the plant was later sold to Texas Instruments. Micron attributed the decision to the continuing fall in 3D NAND prices and to the hard changes data centers and applications would have to make to take full advantage of the product. Micron instead bet on the open-standard interface CXL, because machine-learning systems made Micron realize that not just CPUs needed more memory—GPUs and AI accelerator ASICs did too. Micron's public exit severely weakened Optane: customers could rely only on Intel as a single source, and Optane was proprietary technology. In July 2022 Intel quietly announced the shutdown of the Optane business on its earnings call.

item.title: Ads Are Machine Learning 1.0: How AppLovin Earned an 84% Margin From It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-allin-广告是机器学习的-1-0-applovin-靠它赚出-84-利润率/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-allin-广告是机器学习的-1-0-applovin-靠它赚出-84-利润率/
item.description: Advertising isn't AI's past tense — it's the earliest and most profitable deployment of deep learning. AppLovin used recommendation models to build an 84% EBITDA margin in the $50 billion mobile game ad market, and became its own best investor with $6 billion in buybacks.
item.content:encoded:
Advertising isn't AI's past tense — it's the earliest and most profitable deployment of deep learning. AppLovin used recommendation models to build an 84% EBITDA margin in the $50 billion mobile game ad market, and became its own best investor with $6 billion in buybacks.

A CEO who almost never gives interviews explains the shared technical roots of advertising and AI, the buyback playbook through a 92% drawdown, and why a Chinese engineering team is an advantage. High information density, worth listening to.

1:02 Mobile game advertising is a $50 billion market
Adam says outsiders underestimate the scale of mobile gaming: over a billion adults play casual mobile games every day, and these people are household decision-makers. Two years ago AppLovin disclosed $11 billion in annual ad spend on its own platform, and it has since grown at roughly 60% year over year, which by rough math puts it at about $20 billion today. But that isn't the whole market — many other ad companies monetize in this ecosystem, so double that number again and the entire mobile game ecosystem spends roughly $50 billion a year on advertising. He notes that not long ago social was also just a $50 billion opportunity.

3:02 Advertising is machine learning's earliest and most profitable implementation
Adam calls advertising ML 1.0: it was the first deployment of all the technology that now drives AI. Large language models create more economic value today than advertising, but advertising is an extremely profitable implementation of deep learning models. Recommendation systems and large language models have different architectures, but their trajectories are highly similar — research in large language models can transfer to recommendation systems and vice versa; many large language model researchers spent the early part of their careers looking at ad systems. The beauty of the ad business is that you build a model to predict a future outcome, and the value of that prediction can be converted into money immediately.

6:03 Search ads don't create economic expansion; discovery ads do
Adam divides advertising into two categories. One is bottom-of-funnel advertising: the consumer already knows what they want to buy and is just doing research to complete the transaction — that's Google Search's business, and large language models will compete with Google Search almost entirely in that area. The other is his area: not knowing user intent, creating a demand that didn't exist, so that when users see it they think ‘this looks really cool, I want to buy it right now’. He stresses that the transaction in search or in a large language model was going to happen anyway, so there isn't much economic expansion there; discovery advertising creates economic expansion, which is what makes Meta's ad business strong and what AppLovin wants to do.

8:07 Your phone isn't listening, but your behavior is tracked
Faced with the question of ‘I talk about something at lunch and then an ad appears’, Adam says it's more likely you did something trackable earlier — a search, browsing a website, searching for a product — without realizing it, and then you said something related and started seeing related ads. He states clearly that AppLovin does not track location at all, arguing that tracking precise location to render ads is a very heavy concept, and that the data transfer required to parse microphone content in real time and translate it into ads is unrealistic. But he acknowledges that if you're on a social network, relationship data between you and others can of course drive the ad experience — for example, a friend searched for something and you might see a related ad, which he thinks is fine.

10:07 From $28 billion to $3.8 billion, then it started buying itself
AppLovin went public in April 2021 with $600 million in EBITDA at a market cap of about $28 billion, peaking at $40 billion. In 2022 the stock fell almost every day, down to a market cap of about $3.8 billion — in a year when the company did $1 billion in EBITDA. Adam's read: market cap is determined by the quality of investors, and at the time a lot of companies were going public at the same time, blue-chip investors hadn't done the research to figure out what this company with the silly name was, so there was no demand and a lot of supply, and the valuation fell from 50x EBITDA to under 4x. His response was to stop talking to investors and instead aggressively buy back stock with the large amounts of cash the company generated, eventually buying about $6 billion of its own shares and retiring 20% to 25% of the float.

12:07 When the stock fell 92%, family called to ask if you wanted to kill yourself
Adam says that period was hard, family and friends would call to ask if he wanted to kill himself, and his answer was that the stock was still at $10, still up a lot. But the truly hard part was realizing that as CEO, his team was getting the same calls, and they didn't have his composure or his equity. So they rallied the team with a ‘we versus the world’ mentality, and extended a performance stock program usually reserved for the CEO to key people across the company, telling them: it's hard right now, the house you thought you had is gone, but if you hold on and recover, the upside is huge. Later investors started coming back, the company switched from regression models to deep learning models, the ad algorithm got better, advertiser returns got better, and the business started growing fast.

14:08 A week in New York took the market cap from $28 billion to $55 billion
When the new model launched in April 2023 the company still wasn't communicating with investors, so the outside world didn't know. By around September 2023 the stock was at $80 with good results, and Adam judged the market cap high enough that he couldn't buy back that aggressively anymore, so he went to New York and started talking to investors. That very week the stock went from $80 to $150, and the market cap went from $28 billion to $55 billion — just because he went out and said ‘our company is still here, we survived’. He describes sitting in meetings and being able to read the person across the table texting a friend to buy. Over the next two and a half years the stock went from $9 to $750, and the market cap reached $250 billion. His conclusion is that public market investors and private investors aren't that different, both chase trends, just often later than you'd like.

16:09 After privacy rules tightened, users complained ads got worse
Adam says in these areas you want regulatory clarity, and once the rules are clear, technology can respond. Five years ago you could precisely target users on iOS; today if users say no precise targeting, you can only bundle them into groups and serve worse ads. The interesting result of this change is that after Apple's changes the company received a flood of user complaints saying ‘show me more relevant ads, you're showing me a bunch of garbage now’. So he offers a duality: on one hand you need privacy regulation so tech companies know what to do, on the other hand consumers do want relevant ads — you watch a 30-second ad in a game to get a life, that's something with monetary value, and you don't want to spend those 30 seconds watching garbage.

item.title: Buffets Weren't Eaten to Death — They Were Hollowed Out by the Supermarket Deli
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-modernmba-自助餐不是被吃垮的-是被超市熟食区掏空的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-modernmba-自助餐不是被吃垮的-是被超市熟食区掏空的/
item.description: The 1980s buffet was propped up by cheap food, cheap land, cheap labor and stagnant wages. When all four inputs got more expensive, what actually killed it was the supermarket deli counter eating the low-price market at zero customer-acquisition cost.
item.content:encoded:
The 1980s buffet was propped up by cheap food, cheap land, cheap labor and stagnant wages. When all four inputs got more expensive, what actually killed it was the supermarket deli counter eating the low-price market at zero customer-acquisition cost.

It dissects one industry's cause of death using three public companies' financials and bankruptcy filings — the mechanism is clear and the numbers are solid, and the back half on supermarket deli counters is the most valuable part.

0:02 The buffet deleted everything hard about running a restaurant
The real leap of the 1980s buffet was upgrading "unlimited" from a side dish to the entire business model. It cut every hard part of a traditional restaurant: no servers to hire, no menu to design, almost no English required, no precision needed. The only job was cooking in bulk, heating frozen appetizers, and slicing factory cake into portions. Compared with a regular restaurant where every dish has to earn back its own price, a buffet only has to keep the trays from going empty. Lower skill threshold, a concept that sells itself, one family able to run the whole kitchen, customers serving themselves — the whole model ran on volume. Within a decade, nearly every small town in the Midwest had a Chinese buffet.

8:07 Opening restaurants and keeping customers are two different businesses
Buffets Inc.'s Old Country and Hometown had the simplest strategy: this model doesn't need improvement, it needs replication. From one store to 200 in a decade, doubling again in five years, at its peak opening more than one a week, and after the 1996 merger the largest and fastest buffet operator in the world, with annual revenue near a billion dollars. But fast success created a fatal blind spot — they built the muscle to open buffets, not the muscle to keep customers. The two chains had no real brand, no signature dish, no trademarked recipe; they competed on price and on the volume of advertising rather than its quality. The company bet everything on "scale itself compounds," and a 17% restaurant-level margin in the early 1990s meant nobody dared question the playbook.

9:07 Same-store sales fell for five straight years and nobody knew why
In 1994 same-store sales turned negative and stayed red for five consecutive years; sales were flat for over a decade and lost ground to inflation. Nothing about the restaurants themselves had changed: nearly 40% of the two chains' locations had been opened or remodeled in the previous two years, price increases were small, and after the merger there was no competitor left. But the traffic simply stopped coming, as if Americans had suddenly had enough starting in the mid-1990s, and the format and the chain's novelty faded for no clear reason. The company tried fix after fix, all of them one-year band-aids: in 1995 it cut advertising below 1% of sales to buy profit, and the next year posted the worst same-store sales in its history; only tripling the ad budget turned same-store sales positive — meaning it had to keep marketing and sacrifice margin just to get people through the door.

11:07 Six years under private equity and traffic never improved once
In 2000 a New York private equity firm borrowed more than $500 million to take Buffets Inc. private. The spreadsheet logic was pretty: cut costs, maximize earnings, cover the acquisition debt's interest with cash flow, squeeze the remaining customers, then repackage it for an IPO. But over the six-year holding period traffic never improved. The firm immediately raised prices, cut staff and service, then compensated with promotions, which only alienated customers further and eroded profit. By 2005 the once-healthy company was stuffed with debt, the firm had taken $90 million in dividends for itself, and what was left was a shell paying lenders more in interest than the restaurants earned. Buying Ryan's was just a bigger dose of the same disease — the money came from selling off the land under most of Ryan's restaurants, turning the one asset that didn't depend on traffic into a new annual rent bill.

15:09 No meat was Fresh Choice's profit itself
Fresh Choice tried to solve the economics from the other end: replace expensive protein, which drives up food cost, with cheap salad and carbs. It charged the same prices in Northern California as Old Country and Hometown did in Ohio, yet its food cost stayed 10% below its competitors' — that gap was the entire profit. But customers consistently refused to pay more without a real main course, and every investment meant to justify a price increase only accelerated the churn. The company couldn't give in either, because "no meat" was precisely where its profit came from. It tried uniform pricing, eliminating discounts, adding chicken to the salad, launching thicker soups, designing smaller and cheaper new store formats — none of it worked. By the late 1990s, falling traffic plus a complete lack of pricing power dragged the company into annual losses and penny-stock territory.

21:14 Even the most efficient operator went down all the same
Sweet Tomatoes was the most efficient, most disciplined operator in the industry, and it still came apart. From the start it made itself a destination: standalone restaurants with private parking on land it owned, rather than renting in strip malls like its rivals. Each store had a 55-foot salad bar, eight made-from-scratch soups, a baked potato bar, a dessert bar, a pasta station and a bakery, and from the 1980s it pushed signature items like tuna tarragon and Joan's broccoli madness — branded dishes that injected crucial credibility. For sites it picked business districts and near shopping centers that could capture both lunch and dinner, buying land where it could and otherwise locking in 30-year leases. It also centralized on both ends, prep and stores, building 19 central kitchens to make food fresh in bulk and distribute it to each location, and siting new stores near central kitchens during expansion to keep capacity utilized. But logic and discipline only delayed the inevitable.

24:14 What killed the buffet was the supermarket deli counter
The way the three giants died was no coincidence: Fresh Choice had the cheapest food and died because customers wouldn't pay more than $7 for dinner; Sweet Tomatoes ran the most efficiently and survived as long as it did only because it owned the land under its restaurants; Buffets Inc. had the most locations, the cheapest labor and the strongest economies of scale, and still couldn't raise prices without losing customers. And the fast-food and casual chains that had piggybacked on the 1980s were the first to draw the conclusion — by the late 1990s Wendy's, Burger King and KFC had all shut down their salad bars and unlimited bundles, because none of them made money. The real killer came from inside the supermarket: frozen meals never disrupted the buffet, because they're single-serving while a buffet is designed for families; but dinner just moved to the deli counter of the same supermarket. A supermarket doesn't need the deli to support the whole store, it prices by the pound and by the piece, customers already come in weekly for milk and eggs, and the deli is a zero-customer-acquisition-cost cross-sell that also shares labor and overhead.

30:22 None of the buffet's four profit levers would budge
Every restaurant has only four levers to profit: raise prices, shrink portions, cut labor, shrink the footprint. The buffet chains had none of them. They couldn't raise prices, couldn't cut labor, couldn't shrink portions, couldn't shrink the restaurant. Since the 1990s the whole restaurant industry has moved toward "do more in less space," but a buffet can never be truly efficient — it needs those square feet to hold the variety that makes it appealing, and once it goes big it has to stay big. That worked in the 1980s, when land was cheap, malls were sprouting everywhere, and landlords cared more about traffic than rent. But as malls fell out of favor, retail migrated, and e-commerce hollowed out strip centers, these chains found themselves locked into 10,000-square-foot boxes nobody wanted. That's why the chains filed Chapter 11 over and over — bankruptcy was the only legal way to escape hundreds of leases no one would take over.

item.title: More Collaboration Makes You Slower: Counterintuitive Management from the Product Chiefs at Snap and Discord
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-lennys-协作越多越慢-snap-和-discord-产品一号位反直觉管理法/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-lennys-协作越多越慢-snap-和-discord-产品一号位反直觉管理法/
item.description: Collaboration has hidden costs nobody has internalized, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So Peter Sellis deliberately internalizes collaboration costs aggressively, rather than defaulting to more collaboration being better.
item.content:encoded:
Collaboration has hidden costs nobody has internalized, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So Peter Sellis deliberately internalizes collaboration costs aggressively, rather than defaulting to more collaboration being better.

High information density, but the second half is worth more than the first. For people who want to hear how a product leader actually makes decisions, not for people who want specific growth playbooks.

6:07 More collaboration makes the system slower
Peter says you will never hear an executive say ‘stop collaborating’, and to him that is precisely a warning sign. Collaboration brings enormous coordination costs, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So he deliberately and aggressively internalizes collaboration costs, rather than defaulting to more collaboration being better. This is also where his ‘design teams like a terrorist organization’ idea comes from: one ideological culture that makes everyone understand why they are doing this thing, plus a very clear organizational structure that specifies who can be trusted to make which decision. With those two things, you do not need to over-collaborate, and you still get results that feel ‘as if you had collaborated’.

16:12 The median PM gap is a mathematical structure problem
Peter offers a distributional explanation: product management ability is normally distributed in the population, and the people who actually become PMs are cut from the right tail, and once you cut it, it becomes a power-law distribution, and the median of a power-law distribution is far below the mean. Layer on two more mechanisms: in the ZERP era it became the most lucrative career in tech for people without a technical background, and the definition is subjective, so the people who get in have extremely strong incentives to stay; while the genuinely strong ones have skills that fit almost perfectly into other executive roles or starting their own companies, so ‘great product managers are exiting the system’. Squeezed from both ends, the median is naturally bad. He also points out that the people actually complaining about PMs are the middle cohort of engineers — great engineers know how to bend a PM into the shape they want, and especially bad engineers can hide behind the PM's decisions.

21:16 Snap's ads could not scale for three mathematical reasons
First, users are extremely young, and between 17 and 18, and between 18 and 21, there is a ‘suspicious discontinuity’ in ad CPMs in and outside the US; the rules for tracking, measuring and targeting under-17s are extremely strict, and what is hard to measure is hard to build performance products around. Second, almost all non-search display advertising runs on a screen that exists to show ads, whereas Snap opens to a camera — in the core flow of taking a snap and sending it to a friend, there is no logical place to put an ad; it is a creation-oriented product, not a consumption-oriented one. Third, it is fundamentally a messaging app, and there is currently no good messaging ad product; Asian chat apps get cited repeatedly, but broken down by ‘dollars spent per unit of time’, none of them does particularly well.

35:25 Taste is the nerve to leave good things on the shelf
Peter says one thing he learned at Snap: he watched Evan say no to ideas that were better than what almost any other consumer startup shipped. He describes the product leader's goal as turning the founder into the world's richest museum curator — what is currently on display in the product is only a small part of the whole collection, the pieces the curator judged right for this time and place. He offers a way to probe taste in interviews: ask the person about something they built but never shipped, not something killed because the data was bad, but something they held as a prototype and then judged ‘the world isn't ready’ or ‘this thing isn't ready’. If a museum hung its entire collection on the walls, the curator would have done nothing.

40:29 Advertising is the internet's product-market fit
Peter comes down squarely on Eric Seufert's side: advertising is the internet's product-market fit, and subscription consumer products are overrated. He judges OpenAI to have ‘last mover advantage’ in ads — Meta already solved the modern ad auction as a ‘solved problem’ from 2010 to 2020, and OpenAI is just running through each component quickly. Mechanically he names the modified VCG (Vickrey-Clarke-Groves) auction: it is not the highest bidder who wins, but rather the advertiser's natural value for that user is folded into the bid, so whoever bids high has to pay more to reach people who do not want to be reached. This mechanism lets organic content and ad content go into the same auction, with dollars as the common denominator.

42:30 In chat, the denominator for ads is trust, not relevance
Peter replaces ‘natural value’ in VCG with ‘trust’ in the chat context. A user asks ‘which microphone should I buy’, and the product has to decide whether to give an objective answer, a set of answers, or an advertiser-influenced one — and the degree of influence should equal how much trust you are willing to trade away. He cites Amazon search as an example: search for something and you have to scroll past 16 ads before the first real result, which subtly erodes users' trust in the system. So OpenAI's real deciding factor is not whether to do ads, but how to mathematically maximize long-term trust inside the auction mechanism — trust maximization is very likely correlated with user retention, and may even be causal.

50:35 Growth comes from the core, not from new markets
Verified twice at Snap and Discord: network-effect businesses want to grow on their own, and the most effective move is to serve better — faster, more relevantly — the people already using the product, or wanting to use it, for what it is actually for. He explains with eighth-grade math: it takes 30 monthly actives to equal one daily active, so consumer products should optimize the DAU/MAU ratio, and moving that ratio a few basis points is far more worthwhile than pulling in a pile of new MAUs and gambling on retention. Snap's lesson came from the disastrous 2018 redesign, the only quarter in Snap's overall DAU history that went flat quarter over quarter; after that the team ground away at Android performance, producing a growth revival that lasted years. Discord's version is more counterintuitive: at the time Midjourney was built on Discord, and outsiders all thought this was Discord's big opportunity, but Peter says if you pull up the Discord usage curve, you simply cannot pick out the Midjourney segment.

1:02:44 SpaceX is burning its own ships by hand
Peter considers SpaceX the greatest company right now, and the most worth learning from is how it fights the future: Falcon 9 is the world's best reusable launch system, other countries would trade GDP for it, and yet SpaceX announced it will stop selling Falcon 9 seats in a few years and shift to Starship. He calls this a Cortez-level ship-burning, a way to avoid what Christensen called the innovator's dilemma — because even holding the best thing, you are still willing to build the thing that makes your current product irrelevant. He also notes that SpaceX and Tesla publish ten-year plans openly on their websites, and Tesla even opens its patents; that confidence — ‘I tell you what to do, and if you think you can do it better, come copy it’ — is what he aspires to as a product leader.

item.title: They Tried to Give Hip-Hop's Pioneers Their Money. Some Thought It Was a Scam.
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-a16z-给嘻哈元老发钱-他们以为是诈骗/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-a16z-给嘻哈元老发钱-他们以为是诈骗/
item.description: Some didn't even show up to collect, because they didn't believe it was real. Handing cash out directly doesn't work in hip-hop — in Nas's telling, you have to give recognition and dignity first, and only then can the money be accepted.
item.content:encoded:
Some didn't even show up to collect, because they didn't believe it was real. Handing cash out directly doesn't work in hip-hop — in Nas's telling, you have to give recognition and dignity first, and only then can the money be accepted.

This isn't an investment interview; it's a roundtable on how to pay back a debt owed to a culture. Worth hearing if you care about distribution mechanisms in the creator economy, or if you want to know what Ben Horowitz is actually busy with in private.

2:04 A $10 album owed $5 million
The starting point is a debt Ben Horowitz owed himself: he bought the album Paid in Full for $10 back then, and over his career he got at least $5 million of value out of that record, with no channel to pay it back — and he felt he had to. He called Steve Stoute first, and Steve said the idea wasn't just good, it was timely: everyone was saying these old rappers were broke and dusty, but nobody was actually doing anything. The second call went to Nas, who said Quincy Jones's Jazz Foundation model wouldn't work in hip-hop: you can't just give a person money, it has to be recognition of what he did and who he is, it has to be more than money. So the form became an awards ceremony and a Grandmaster Award, with Scarface and Rakim honored in the first batch.

5:05 Some thought it was a scam and didn't come collect
The foundation's first obstacle wasn't money, it was that nobody believed it. Ben says the level of disbelief early on exceeded imagination, and for a while they even had a hard time actually getting the money into people's hands — some didn't show up to accept the award because they thought it was a scam, and others said "I don't need someone giving me money." He treats that disbelief as evidence the design was right: it can't look like compensation, it has to be celebration and tribute, shining the light they deserve on them, and only then will it be accepted. Caz later put it more bluntly: the industry has shortchanged these people for so long that the first reaction can only be "why would anyone help us now."

10:07 The first hip-hop hit was stolen from him
Grandmaster Caz wrote the rhyme that became Rapper's Delight, his own name was even in the rhyme, and the first hip-hop hit was taken out of his hands just like that, and he never got what he was owed. Ben says everyone in the music industry knows this, but nobody has ever done anything, and nobody has ever said anything. The first time he met Caz in New York he was stunned: this is a man who changes the energy of any room he walks into today, and he carries not a trace of resentment, still thinking of himself as a star. Steve added one line: it's not that nobody knows, it's that not enough people know — the industry knows, the public doesn't.

17:10 Dr. Dre asked for an introduction to his idol
Steve Stoute told one detail: Dr. Dre heard about Paid in Full and decided to come, then asked whether Steve could introduce him to Kool Moe Dee — Dre had never met him. Another time in Las Vegas, Dre again asked whether he could be introduced to Slick Rick, whom he had likewise never met. A Dre who has made it has to ask someone for an introduction just to meet these legends, which shows how fragmented the scene is cut — and getting these people into one room was something only this foundation managed to do. Caz put it more directly: the industry separates people by success, status, who's hot right now; for years he only ran into Nas by chance, and now they see each other once a year and can call each other.

32:20 The Grammys botched it, so they did it themselves
Quincy Jones was the legend of legends in these people's minds, but when he died the Grammy tribute was called out flatly as botched. The Quincy Jones Award wasn't conceived to fill a slot — it came from seeing the Grammys get it wrong, and Quincy's son QD3 saying then let's do it ourselves, and only then did it become an award the foundation gives out every year. This year's recipient is Nile Rodgers. Steve mentioned that George Clinton showed up last year, brought his "mothership" prop, and at 83 recited the lyrics to Rakim's Follow the Leader on stage — a man who changed music, paying tribute to another man who changed music.

39:24 Hip-hop has no social security
Caz explained what this money concretely means: it's a grant paid out over five years, and he bought a house and moved out of the projects. He lived in the Bronx his whole life, and for the past ten to fifteen years his last thought in his head was always "I don't want to die in the projects"; now he and his wife live in a house in Pennsylvania. He says hip-hop has no social security, no health insurance, you have to keep working, so the reason you still see him doing radio, doing park shows, doing hip-hop tours is that he has to. This money gave him something he never had: a buffer. He also made a point of saying money is only part of this, and the real thing is being put in the light.

44:26 Brands came back from the dead on hip-hop
Steve Stoute used business data to explain why "paying the debt" is reasonable: Adidas had only 2% market share in the US at the time, three-quarters of it from the Northeast, and the company only saw a bunch of people frantically buying the same shoe and throwing the laces away, with no idea why. Grand Puba's lyric "First things first, obey your thirst" later became Sprite's ad line. Tommy Hilfiger was selling ties back then and couldn't move them; driving through Harlem he saw everyone wearing their pants low with the Calvin Klein waistband showing, so he went back and made the underwear waistband wider and thicker and printed his own name on it, and only then did the brand take off. These brands exist because of what these people contributed.

48:31 Love isn't writing a check, it's flying to Houston
Ben told a story about his wife, who is also the foundation's chair, Felicia, to illustrate how this organization differs from other charities: Scarface had a heart problem and needed open-heart surgery, but he came from a place where people don't even really go to the doctor, he was afraid to go, and on the phone he said he wasn't going. Felicia flew to Houston and said no, you're going now. Just as they walked into the exam room, his aorta ruptured, and the doctors got him in in time and saved his life. Steve added the everyday version: she'll suddenly call to ask how you and your family are doing, and if someone in your family gets sick, flowers arrive the next day, or whatever was agreed arrives.

item.title: Fashion Mogul: Stop Apologizing for Being a Working Mom, and Talk About Money
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-wsjournal-时尚大亨-当妈不必道歉-钱要开口谈/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-wsjournal-时尚大亨-当妈不必道歉-钱要开口谈/
item.description: Emma Grede says if women avoid talking about money, money will avoid them; by talking about money proactively, picking the right partners, and doing the business others can't be bothered to do, she turned overlooked customers into loyal repeat buyers.
item.content:encoded:
Emma Grede says if women avoid talking about money, money will avoid them; by talking about money proactively, picking the right partners, and doing the business others can't be bothered to do, she turned overlooked customers into loyal repeat buyers.

Medium information density. The first half covers brands and partnerships; the second half, on money mindset and maternal guilt, is the more valuable part. Good for a commute.

3:18 A celebrity is an accelerator, not a partner
Grede says that if you throw a star and a brand together expecting to make money or build credibility, you'll quickly find it doesn't hold up. A celebrity can bring one burst of exposure and attention, but they can't keep customers — only a strong loyalty to a good product brings people back. That's why she insists on treating the Kardashian sisters as true business partners, not spokespeople — the partnership has to be bigger than ‘someone's follower count’. She admits she was lucky to find partners capable of doing that.

4:19 Target the market nobody is taking seriously
Grede says before any business she looks at the competitive landscape first, knowing what's declining and what might be needed. When Good American entered the plus-size market in 2016, the whole industry treated it as a ‘bonus 15%’ add-on, and even today's talking points didn't exist. She believes it was rewriting the rules completely in a space where nobody was innovating and customers weren't understood that made the company succeed. She stresses she never watches fashion week and doesn't chase trends, because ‘if you're led by trends, you'll die very fast.’

7:28 The harder the business, the more it's worth doing
