Rob said he doesn't understand why Circle came out on day one pushing a bunch of memes, since Arc had always been positioned as a payments-first chain, talking about agentic finance, privacy, FX liquidity, real commercial activity. He said this is the exact opposite of the story Circle has long told, and it left a lot of people with a bad impression. Santi said he went to Circle's launch event yesterday, and the room and Twitter were two completely different worlds — within an hour he met people from BlackRock, DTCC, ICE, Visa, MoneyGram, and Circle's convening power is extremely strong; if they had launched purely on the original positioning, it would have gone much better. Rob said Circle may have seen Robinhood chain's success, but Robinhood is a trading platform and Circle is a payments company, and having bought Taza Pay it should stay in its own lane.

42:38 Circle's revenue gets cut in half by rates
Rob said he doesn't expect 4% to 4.5% rates to last forever, and that rates will normalize to between 2% and 3%, which means if Circle is just an interest-income business, its revenue at current TVL gets cut in half. He also said that as a payments stablecoin, if you can't share yield with end customers, there isn't much reason to hold large amounts of it. Circle's agreement with Coinbase requires giving 50% to Coinbase, which puts it at a disadvantage competing with new stablecoins. So Circle is working to become a payments company and get a payments company multiple, and Arc and Circle Payment Network are both part of that story. Santi said don't underestimate USDC's network effect — in DeFi there is now only one thing that matters for liquidity, and that's USDC; every DeFi founder needs USDC on their platform.

46:14 Instinct's reckoning comes in month four
Rob said companies are now getting bigger faster and raising more faster, that venture capital as a market structure is broken, and that the hottest companies see valuations rise faster and faster regardless of fundamentals. He said a company's first big reckoning usually comes in year four, but Instinct's first big reckoning will come in month four — because the two biggest companies in the world are about to ship direct competitors, Grokbot and Meta's Muse. Santi said from his own use Muse is six to eight times better than Instinct; Instinct is clearly compute-constrained, Muse is sometimes 10 to 15 minutes faster on the same question, fails less, and can route around the roadblocks Resy set up for these products. Rob said he doesn't know how growth investors are comfortable at this valuation, and the only thing that could prove them wrong is Instinct sprinting to train its own model, but that takes a billion dollars to build data centers.

item.title: Prediction Markets Aren't Casinos, but 90% of Volume Comes From Sports
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freakonomics-预测市场不是赌场-但九成交易量来自体育/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freakonomics-预测市场不是赌场-但九成交易量来自体育/
item.description: Kalshi traded four years of compliance for 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a bookmaker's; what's genuinely underrated are the quiet markets like FDA approvals.
item.content:encoded:
Kalshi traded four years of compliance for 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a bookmaker's; what's genuinely underrated are the quiet markets like FDA approvals.

The first half is founder narrative; the value is in the middle and back: how contracts are written, the 90% sports share, regulatory risk. Worth listening for anyone who wants to understand how prediction markets actually work.

8:16 Comply for four years first, then open your first market
Kalshi's two founders wrote "regulatory first" into the company's principles and spent four years getting regulatory approval before launching their first market. Mansoor calls this anti-Silicon Valley: everyone else builds the product and patches in compliance later, while they went to the federal government first and asked, "How should this be regulated?" The cost was that for the first four years he wanted to quit almost every day, held up by the fact that "the cost of regret is too high." The payoff came in 2024, when a federal appeals court ruled Kalshi could list election contracts, landing just before the presidential election. Mansoor attributes the 90% market share directly to that path: institutions would rather plug into a platform that's inside the system, because changing the rules from outside the system is harder.

15:36 Prediction markets force you to shut up, not to take a position
Robin Hanson lays out three mechanisms that make prediction markets more accurate than polls or expert interviews. First, people being interviewed have an incentive to be interesting, dramatic, and to tell the questioner what they want to hear, while the market only rewards being right. Second, the market gives you an incentive to shut up about topics you don't understand — you'll only pick the handful of markets where you genuinely have an edge, whereas interviewees will answer confidently on things they know nothing about. Third, the market doesn't require you to have a direct opinion on a topic; it invites you to find mispricings and errors in other people's pricing, and pays you to correct them. He closes with an old poker-table line: sit down and look for the sucker; if you can't find him, you're the sucker — so don't play that market.

20:48 Internal prediction markets die on the project owner's excuse
Eli Lilly ran an internal prediction market in the early 2000s that successfully predicted which drug compounds would pass Phase III trials; Google ran one too, called Google Profit. Both were judged effective, and neither survived. Hanson's explanation: the project owner wants to know whether they'll deliver on time, but what they want even more is a good excuse if they fail. And the best excuse is precisely "everything was going fine, and then at the last minute something happened that nobody could have anticipated." A market that continuously and accurately predicts "will you be late" voids that excuse in advance, so nobody wants it to exist.

22:58 Domain expertise is not the key skill for forecasting the future
Mansoor cites Philip Tetlock's Superforecasting research: put experts in a given domain — geopolitics, say — up against a group of non-experts forecasting the same set of events, and the non-experts win. His explanation is that domain experts become too doctrinaire over time, while people who can step back and look at things coolly are better calibrated and less biased. Mansoor says this is a fairly heretical claim in politics, academia, and financial analysis — it implies that if you want a more accurate answer, you should look for a diverse group of participants who pride themselves on self-calibration, critical reading, and filtering information, not an authority in some field. He treats this as Kalshi's underlying logic.

33:28 One contract takes a month to write, for grammar and apostrophes
Nicole Kagan writes the contracts and self-certifies them with the CFTC. The most complex category is "what someone will say in a given speech," and they recently rewrote the rules because a pile of grammar questions came up: what if there's an apostrophe? If they misspeak or mispronounce it, does it still count as the same word? What if it appears inside a proper noun? What if the livestream cuts out midway and the video is uploaded somewhere else afterward? Those rules took over a month to write, run seven or eight pages, and are extremely detailed. When Bloomberg reported on them, it guessed they were built for automated processing and must be for AI; Kagan says that's not it at all — they wrote them so users could understand, and never considered that "anything a human can understand, a computer probably can too."

35:35 When you can't call a winner, settle at the last fair price
Kalshi's contracts are usually binary: pay $1 if the event happens, $0 if it doesn't, with every position fully collateralized — if one side stakes 30 cents, someone must stake 70. But some situations can't be judged yes or no. Cardi B was clearly dancing during her seven-second Super Bowl halftime cameo, but she had no mic and there was no way to confirm whether she was singing, so the team said "we are epistemically uncertain" and settled at the last fair price. Another case is 50-50: when multiple people win simultaneously, each settles at 50 cents. Kagan says they have the right to do this when it's "genuinely unclear" whether an event meets the criteria, and they've already revised the halftime contract — the new rules require an audible lead or backing vocal, and under those rules Cardi B didn't perform.

41:52 Ninety percent of volume comes from sports, and that's the most uncomfortable fact
Dubner puts it bluntly: roughly 90% of Kalshi's volume is concentrated in a category barely mentioned until then — sports, the business that makes DraftKings and FanDuel nervous. Mansoor's response is that the sports share is falling fast and other categories are growing faster, but he concedes that "10% is also a lot, and don't forget we're big." He insists on distinguishing gambling from trading: all derivatives markets are mostly speculative, speculation provides liquidity, and the key isn't whether speculation exists but the business model — one model hunts for losers and bans winners, the other pursues price discovery and wants smart people in. He also concedes the second model carries risk, saying there is "responsible gambling" and "responsible trading," and that platforms have a responsibility to monitor.

44:00 Seventy to eighty percent of active users never place an order
Mansoor says one of his favorite numbers is this: 70% to 80% of active users don't trade. They just log in every day, keep it next to X and alongside a few newspapers, and use it to calibrate or check information. Kalshi's business model is a neutral platform, like the NYSE or Nasdaq, taking an average 1% on trades and not caring who wins or loses. He also says the information environment is getting more polarized and the signal-to-noise ratio is falling, because social media algorithms reward clickbait: write a nuanced, restrained, multi-paragraph take on X and you get four likes; write something wildly outrageous and you get tens of thousands. Prediction markets have exactly the opposite incentive — the nuanced, boring, well-calibrated judgment is the one that makes money.

item.title: Diffusion Isn't Just for Images — It Wants to Win Inference for Language Models
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-nopriors-扩散模型不是图像专利-它要在推理时赢下语言模型/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-nopriors-扩散模型不是图像专利-它要在推理时赢下语言模型/
item.description: Autoregressive inference must generate one token at a time, sequentially, and is memory-bandwidth bound; diffusion models process multiple tokens in parallel, so the inference workload looks more like training — which is why Inception is betting on it.
item.content:encoded:
Autoregressive inference must generate one token at a time, sequentially, and is memory-bandwidth bound; diffusion models process multiple tokens in parallel, so the inference workload looks more like training — which is why Inception is betting on it.

A diffusion-model founder explains clearly why parallelism at inference becomes the deciding factor in architecture, and how a 50-person company finds differentiation in the gap between giants.

3:10 Diffusion started because GANs were too unstable
Ermon says that when he was working on image generation back then, he was very dissatisfied with GANs: they worked, but training was extremely unstable and results were hard to reproduce. So in 2019 he and his PhD students turned to score-based generative models, with the idea of training a neural network to denoise — if it can denoise, that means it understands image structure, and it can then work in reverse to progressively refine a clean image out of pure noise. This is the underlying technology of modern diffusion models. He stresses that today's best image, video, some music, and a large number of protein models are all based on diffusion.

5:11 The 2024 paper moved diffusion onto text
Ermon's team published a paper in 2024 that, for the first time at GPT-2 scale (under a billion parameters), got a diffusion model to match autoregressive model quality: the same perplexity, the same degree of data fit, but roughly 10x faster generation, because diffusion outputs multiple tokens at once. He says this was still fairly academic, but it was enough for him to decide to start a company and scale the technology to commercial size.

8:14 Autoregressive inference is a memory-bandwidth bottleneck
Ermon likens the 2017 switch from RNNs to transformers to the inference stage: during training, transformers won by processing multiple tokens in parallel, but at inference the autoregressive model is still sequential — before generating the 10th token it must first generate all the preceding tokens. This workload is extremely memory-bandwidth limited; most of the time goes to moving weights between levels of the memory hierarchy, with very little arithmetic, which is unfriendly to GPUs. Diffusion models' inference workload looks more like training — processing multiple tokens in parallel at once — so it naturally matches the compute pattern GPUs are good at.

10:16 Inference efficiency also caps RL post-training
Ermon points out that economics are determined by how much intelligence you get per watt and per dollar. Much of the progress in reasoning models comes from test-time compute scaling, and one of the bottlenecks in RL post-training is generating rollouts — letting the model explore, scoring trajectories, then improving the model. So inference efficiency directly gates post-training efficiency: a model that scales better at inference will automatically also scale better during post-training. This is the core logic behind his bet on diffusion LLMs, and what he means by ‘the more parallel approach will eventually win’.

12:19 Mercury is benchmarked against Haiku, Flash, mini
Ermon says Inception's Mercury model is benchmarked against speed-optimized models like Haiku, Flash, and mini nano, with comparable quality but significantly faster, and it is already serving customers in production. He stresses that you cannot run a diffusion LLM directly on vLLM or SGLang — you have to build your own serving engine to handle the complexity of real production workloads. This is both a barrier and a moat: even if someone else trains a diffusion LLM, without a corresponding serving engine they cannot put it to use.

17:21 A voice customer switched from custom chips back to Nvidia GPUs
Ermon gives the example of voice agent company OpenCall: the voice pipeline includes ASR, a reasoning LLM for tool calls, and TTS, and speed is critical. OpenCall originally served its LLM on Cerebras custom chips to reach the required speed, then switched to Inception's diffusion LLM, because it could get the same speed on Nvidia GPUs — higher availability, lower cost, better quality. Ermon says once you get used to a fast model you can't go back, like broadband.

25:26 Diffusion is inherently more controllable than autoregression
Ermon says diffusion models are generally easier to control than autoregressive models: autoregression must wait until the entire object is generated before knowing whether it satisfies constraints, whether it is aligned, what score the reward function gives; diffusion is coarse-to-fine generation, so from early on you can judge whether the direction is right, and you can use external reward functions or constraint sets to guide generation. There is a fair amount of evidence in the academic literature supporting this, and some guidance methods simply cannot be done on autoregressive models. He sees this as the differentiation space for future product experiences.

29:29 20% to 30% of tasks are extremely latency-sensitive
Ermon estimates based on OpenRouter's task categories (research, chat, coding, software engineering, log processing, etc.) that about 20% to 30% of those tasks care a lot about latency. As a lower bound, that portion of the workload can be taken by the model that delivers the highest quality within a given latency budget. He also acknowledges that we are not yet at frontier intelligence, and much of the workload still needs frontier-level intelligence, so the addressable market for diffusion models is layered.

item.title: When Your Kids Fight, Are You a Witness or a Judge?
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-raisinggh-孩子打架时-你是证人还是法官/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-raisinggh-孩子打架时-你是证人还是法官/
item.description: The biggest mistake parents make when stepping into sibling conflict is refereeing with their own childhood fairness wounds. What kids need isn't a verdict on who was right, but practice repairing the relationship inside low-stakes conflict.
item.content:encoded:
The biggest mistake parents make when stepping into sibling conflict is refereeing with their own childhood fairness wounds. What kids need isn't a verdict on who was right, but practice repairing the relationship inside low-stakes conflict.

Medium information density with a clear core framework: witness not judge, sportscaster mode, fairness is not equality. Best for parents with more than one child, especially those whose own childhood emotions get triggered by sibling fights.

3:05 Deal with your own sibling baggage before you step in
The episode opens by pointing out that almost everyone carries sibling baggage — even if you don't have siblings, you carry either a longing for that ‘mythical connection’ or relief at not having it. The fairness trap is the thing most likely to trigger a parent's emotions: a cake sliced unevenly, a rule that was looser for one kid, a new dress given to only one of you — those memories get activated the moment you see your own kids fighting. If you step in before dealing with that baggage, you're effectively imposing your sibling history on your children. So the first step is always clearing your own head, not rushing in to hand down a verdict.

4:07 You are a witness, not a judge
This is the single most important line in the whole piece, and Dr. Pressman repeats it a dozen-plus times. The moment you start deciding who's right, who hit first, who was worse, that judgment comes from your own history, not from what's actually happening between these two kids right now. As a witness, your job is to observe and describe, not to rule. That distinction determines your tone, your words, and your posture when you step in. Once you become the judge, you'll unconsciously favor, convict, and punish — and what your kids feel isn't justice, it's your unfinished childhood emotions making decisions for them.

5:09 When you absolutely must step in
Dr. Pressman gives clear signals for stepping in: a child is in danger, there's a power imbalance, or they're stuck in a loop they can't get out of. If the two are evenly matched and physically safe, you can stay nearby and occasionally ask ‘Is everyone okay?’ But watch especially for power dynamics turning into toxic bullying — it's rare, but when it happens, an adult must cut it off. Kids who've experienced peer or sibling bullying have far worse adult outcomes, and the damage is much bigger than we realize. Bullying has a strict definition, though: a power differential plus repeated, malicious, intentional abuse. Just ‘being a jerk’ isn't bullying, and kids being jerks to each other is completely normal.

6:17 Sportscaster mode: describe, don't adjudicate
If you do need to step in, Dr. Pressman recommends ‘sportscaster mode’ — you act like an observant, reflective commentator who just describes what happened. For example: ‘I noticed this happened over here, and that happened over there — did I get that right?’ This lets you validate both kids at once, without taking sides, without a winner. The key is to avoid questions like ‘Who started it?’ ‘You always do this,’ ‘There's something wrong with you.’ When you tell a child there's something wrong with who they are rather than with a specific behavior, you're feeding the exact habit you don't want them using on each other — turning anger and outbursts into a question about a person's worth. ‘You're stupid’ means ‘You are a stupid person,’ and no one needs to hear that.

8:21 Stop dehumanizing language on the spot
Dr. Pressman says kids can scream, yell, be vicious to each other, even get physical — but if she hears dehumanizing language, she'll pause the fight on the spot to change the wording. Because what you want to constantly ‘wire’ and ‘bake’ into your kids is: talk about the behavior, not about who the person is. This isn't a lesson for later; it's immediate intervention. She'll say in that moment, ‘Let's rephrase that.’ The logic behind it: language habits need repeated reinforcement to internalize, and every dehumanizing expression you let slide is reinforcement in the opposite direction.

14:33 Fairness isn't equality — it's needs-based
Dr. Pressman uses the peanut butter cupcake example to explain the difference between fair and equal: giving two kids peanut butter cupcakes that are exactly the same size and exactly the same recipe looks equal, but if one of them is allergic to peanuts, it's completely unfair. Fair means giving each child what they need, not giving everyone the same thing. This framework protects you when a child demands ‘Why does my 12-year-old sister get a phone and I don't?’ — you can answer, ‘You're different people, I've learned more since then, and I'm making a different decision that's better for you.’ If you try to be perfectly equal, you're assuming every child is the same age, same personality, same temperament, same interests, same needs — which obviously doesn't hold.

16:37 Don't label your kids
Dr. Pressman points out that giving all your kids the same label (like ‘You're all helpers’) does promote positive behavior, but if you give only one child in the family the ‘helper’ label, it creates tension and problematic dynamics. Labels plant seeds of resentment, insecurity, and lack of motivation, and they push siblings apart. Teachers, friends, other parents, relatives — they all label. A parent's job is to counteract that damage, not join in. Labels ‘haunt’ a child — Dr. Pressman uses the word haunt, and says it sounds dramatic but it's true.

18:41 Repair isn't a forced apology
Dr. Pressman distinguishes real repair from fake repair. Repair isn't necessarily a public apology — if after a fight the kids suddenly giggle together, share an inside joke, make faces at each other, that's repair, that's reconnection, and you're witnessing it. Every reconnection strengthens the relationship and teaches kids ‘This relationship is forever, it gets messy, but we always come back.’ But a forced apology isn't repair. Saying ‘I'm sorry’ and saying ‘Apologize to your brother’ don't teach what the research literature calls repair. An insincere apology just makes people angrier. You can ask, ‘How do you think that made your sibling feel? Is there anything you could do to help them feel better?’ If the child says no, you don't just drop it — you come back later and ask, ‘Have you had time to think about that?’

item.title: America's Richest Are Hiding in Small Business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-oddlots-美国最富的一群人-藏在小生意里/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-oddlots-美国最富的一群人-藏在小生意里/
item.description: Half the rise in US income inequality comes from pass-through business income — and the owners aren't tech giants, they're car dealers, beer distributors, dentists and hot dog sellers, protected as "small business" for forty years.
item.content:encoded:
Half the rise in US income inequality comes from pass-through business income — and the owners aren't tech giants, they're car dealers, beer distributors, dentists and hot dog sellers, protected as "small business" for forty years.

A new study built on linked IRS full tax-return data pulls the question of "who are the rich" back from the tech narrative to regional middle-market businesses; high information density, suited to anyone tracking taxes, PE and wealth distribution.

6:13 Tax returns assemble a different picture of the rich
More than a decade ago the two authors were commissioned by the Treasury to link corporate tax returns with the returns of owners and employees, because the IRS itself could not match the different forms belonging to the same business. They found that the picture of the rich painted by the media and by Capital in the Twenty-First Century is very different from the actual picture in US tax returns: not passive rent-collecting Gilded Age monopolists, but millions of actively operating middle-market regional business owners. That data project later became the basis of the book.

12:16 Seventy percent of pass-through income goes to the top 1%
Of pass-through business income, 70 cents of every dollar flows to the top 1% of earners. From the 1980s to 2021, more than half of the rise in the top 1%'s income share came from pass-through business income. So anyone trying to understand income inequality and wealth inequality cannot get around this sector. The authors had assumed monopolistic giants were passively collecting the money; instead they found middle-market regional businesses spread across the whole country, numbering in the millions.

15:22 Car dealers are the single biggest bucket of pass-through income
The book opens with a "wedding of the century": a third-generation Mercedes dealer in Florida threw his daughter's wedding in Paris, renting out Versailles for the dinner, spending $60 million — right after selling the dealership for several hundred million dollars. When the authors looked at top 0.1% pass-through income by industry, car dealers ranked first. They then went to yacht and private jet registration data and found these people by name, because tax returns themselves cannot identify individuals.

19:23 Car dealer wealth is half skill, half license
The authors tell two stories. Larry Miller started in Toyota's parts division, took the parts business from 961st to first, later owned more than 40 dealerships and bought the Utah Jazz — a good case of "move slow and make things." But the other side is regulatory protection: franchise laws were meant to protect small dealers from being force-fed inventory by Ford and GM, yet in 2008 Chrysler had three times as many dealerships as Toyota while selling the same number of cars, and closing a store meant paying three years' rent. Dealers also enjoy geographic monopolies and high margins on add-on services like warranties and financing.

22:25 Beer distributors are a rent-collecting layer left by Prohibition
The truck you see on the road with Budweiser on it actually belongs to a distributor, such as Reyes. These distributors sit between brewers and bars, restaurants and grocery stores; state laws require beer to pass through this layer, originally to stop big brewers from controlling production and distribution at once. The result is that these "little guys" became big guys, showing up in large numbers in the private jet data. The authors mention a beer wholesalers' convention in San Antonio where the mayor said he had never seen so many private jets at the airport.

34:31 Same anesthesiologist, far higher tax burden for the employee
The book contrasts two anesthesiologists: one runs a private practice through an S-Corp, the other draws a salary in a hospital system. The former treats most of his income as business profit, paying no payroll tax and no uncapped Medicare surtax, even though he bills Medicare heavily. The IRS only requires payroll tax on the "reasonable compensation" portion of wages; anything above that counts as profit. The 2017 reform cut the top pass-through rate from 37% to below 30%, and although it put guardrails on professional services like doctors, carving out surgery, ancillary services or real estate can still shift more income into the lower-rate bucket.

38:35 A quarter of federal elected officials are pass-through owners too
The authors say the reason the tax loophole survives so long is that roughly a quarter of federal elected officials are themselves pass-through business owners. Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno is a car dealer, and the Social Security plan he introduced with Elizabeth Warren is funded by a payroll tax on working-class wages, with no mention at all of these wealthy business owners. The authors argue the most realistic reform is not to abolish the loophole but to cap it by income: for instance, once business income exceeds $1 million or $400,000, you can no longer take the deduction that cuts the rate from 37% to 30%.

48:52 The owners' share of the pie went from four-tenths to five-tenths
Over the past 25 years, 60% of growth in the corporate sector came from the pass-through form, so the pie is getting bigger; at the same time the share owners take out of that pie rose from a third to 40% and then to about 50%. Using data from 2001 to 2021, the authors calculate that value added per worker rose from $34,000 to $52,000, a gain of $18,000, of which owners took $15,000. They attribute this to skill scarcity (the US has 30% fewer doctors per capita than the OECD average, with the AMA restricting supply), policy-created scarcity, and the rising value of professional services such as M&A.

item.title: Hair relaxer made Black women beautiful, and made them pay with their health
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ninepi-直发剂让黑人女性变美-也让她们付出健康代价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ninepi-直发剂让黑人女性变美-也让她们付出健康代价/
item.description: Chemical hair relaxer built the Black community's earliest millionaire industry and has also been linked by research to elevated uterine cancer risk — the same product is both an economic ladder and a bodily cost.
item.content:encoded:
Chemical hair relaxer built the Black community's earliest millionaire industry and has also been linked by research to elevated uterine cancer risk — the same product is both an economic ladder and a bodily cost.

This episode has medium information density, but it tells the story of how one product can be empowerment and harm at the same time very concretely — suited to listeners interested in consumer history, public health, and the racial economy.

1:06 Hair relaxer is "creamy crack"
Chemical hair relaxer has a nickname in the salon: creamy crack, because it is said to be as addictive as cocaine — once you start, it is hard to stop. When you stop, the new curly growth breaks off where it meets the already-straightened dead hair. The week before use you cannot wash your hair or scratch your scalp, or you will get burned; when applying it you have to avoid the scalp and coat only the hair shaft, but leaving it too long near the ends still stings. In the episode the host recalls being slathered with relaxer for the first time at age 9, having already seen women in the salon cry out in pain.

5:18 From African hair tradition to a survival strategy
Hair historian Lorie Tharps says starting the story from slavery is starting from chapter two and missing chapter one: Africa already had a rich hair tradition, and hair connected tribe, family, and identity. After being enslaved in America, straightening hair went from self-expression to survival strategy — because they were told their hair was inferior, ugly, more like an animal's, and straightening it became a visual way to prove "we are equal to you." They used butter instead of palm oil, made shampoo from cornmeal and kerosene, used butter knives as crude curling irons, and wrapped hair around yarn to straighten it.

8:21 Barbers' money built Black colleges
The methods these enslaved people invented were good enough to make them the first choice as barbers and wig makers for white people. White people paid for their craft, and this channel let many of them buy their own freedom. Tharps says some early Black colleges and institutions were funded or founded by Black barbers, such as Wilberforce University — an HBCU wholly owned and operated by African Americans, built to a large extent on barbering income. But the irony is that these Black barbers did not cut Black people's hair at the time; they served white clients.

10:22 The hot comb gave way to an accidental discovery
Madame CJ Walker and Annie Turnbo Malone used the hot comb plus hair oil to produce sleek straight hair, turning scattered straightening methods into a system, and Walker became the first self-made millionaire woman in America, of any race. But the hot comb's effect was temporary, reverting with sweat, moisture, or rain. In the early 1900s, Cleveland tailor Garrett Augustus Morgan wanted to invent a substance that kept high-speed machines and needles from damaging wool and other animal fur, and after trying a formula he found the fur had straightened. He first tested it on a neighbor's dog, then on his own hair, and both straightened — he had accidentally discovered that lye (sodium hydroxide) plus other ingredients could straighten hair.

14:24 The man who put relaxer on drugstore shelves
George Johnson is called by Tharps the Madam CJ Walker of his era. A barber who made homemade conks came to this chemist and asked whether he could make something fast and easy, and that produced Ultra Wave for men, followed by Ultra Sheen for women. Unlike the temporary hot comb and dangerous homemade lye formulas, Ultra Sheen was long-lasting, safer, and available at any drugstore, with no need to go to a salon. That privacy was crucial: straightening hair with chemicals carried shame, and doing it at home meant no one saw you going to the salon.

16:26 Profits flowed back to the Black community, then regulators took notice
Johnson put profits back into the Black community: Soul Train, Essence Magazine, Chicago's Independence Bank — then the largest Black-owned bank in the country, lending to homeowners and entrepreneurs redlined by white banks; funding Martin Luther King Jr. and Jesse Jackson; employing hundreds of Black and brown workers who could not find jobs because of racial discrimination, giving them profit sharing, full health insurance, on-site nurses, full college tuition, paid maternity and sick leave, and four-day weekends every holiday. In 1964 Johnson Products became the first Black-owned company listed on the American Stock Exchange. But in 1975 the FTC required Johnson to put a warning label on the outside of relaxer packaging, saying the product contained lye and could be harmful — while Revlon's relaxer, which also contained lye, was not immediately required to add a label, and the delay ran nearly two years.

20:28 The civil rights movement flipped the politics of straight hair
During the Black Power movement, Black people decided straight hair had solved nothing — from Madam CJ Walker's straightening comb to relaxer, every method had been tried, and it still had not worked. So came a simpler and more radical idea: I will no longer straighten my hair, I will use my hair as protest. Black hair grows up and out, and it does not make you smaller — it makes you taller. The political flip was so complete that some Black people with naturally straight hair got perms to curl it, because not everyone's hair can grow into an Angela Davis-style afro. But the beauty industry then commodified the afro, selling wigs and marketing it as beauty and empowerment while also pulling its teeth, turning it into just another fashion trend. By the 1980s, straight hair was back.

28:38 A 34,000-woman study: risk up two and a half times
A large 2022 study followed 34,000 women and found that frequent users of chemical hair straightening products — most of them Black women — were two and a half times as likely to develop uterine cancer as never-users. New York Times Magazine contributor Linda Varosa says this was the first high-quality study to link straightening products, Black women, and two cancers (endometrial cancer and uterine cancer). The study also linked these products to fibroids, and Black women have fibroids at far higher rates than other women. The study shows correlation, not causation, but Tharps thinks agonizing over correlation versus causation misses the point: she thinks the red flag should be waved directly, with warnings on packaging, labels, and in salons.

item.title: A Broken Arm Forced a French Perfect Score: Constraints Are the Engine of Creativity
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-cautionary-断臂逼出的法语满分-限制才是创造力的引擎/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-cautionary-断臂逼出的法语满分-限制才是创造力的引擎/
item.description: After David Epstein broke his arm, he was forced to use image-based memory instead of shorthand, and his French score hit perfect. A two-day London Underground strike led many people to find better commutes. Constraints aren't obstacles—they're switches that force experimentation.
item.content:encoded:
After David Epstein broke his arm, he was forced to use image-based memory instead of shorthand, and his French score hit perfect. A two-day London Underground strike led many people to find better commutes. Constraints aren't obstacles—they're switches that force experimentation.

Medium information density. The core is the framework distinguishing useful constraints from useless ones. The second half on scientific integrity and entrepreneurial experimentation is more valuable than the first.

5:28 A broken arm forced a memory method
In eighth grade, David Epstein was playing American football and threw the ball too hard; his arm broke on the follow-through, and his right arm was bound from shoulder to hand against his torso. He originally had weekly dictation tests in French class: listen to a native speaker's recording and fill in blanks in a text. His scores were mediocre. After his right hand was bound, he couldn't write fast enough with his left, so he had to hold the flying words in his mind first, linking each word to something sports-related—he didn't know then that this was called a mnemonic device. As a result, he could remember every word, then slowly fill them in with his left hand, and started getting perfect scores. The key mechanism: his most convenient path was blocked, forcing him to find an alternative, and the alternative was better.

8:35 A two-day subway strike improved commutes for years
During a London Underground strike, people were forced to find different routes to work. The strike lasted only 48 hours, but a significant portion of people discovered a better commute than the one they had used for weeks, months, or even years, and continued using it afterward. Epstein recalls the study saying this collectively saved about 1,500 hours of commuting time per day. His inference: we normally experiment too little; useful constraints drive people to run experiments they otherwise wouldn't, and the gains from those experiments can far exceed the inconvenience.

10:38 General Magic died from too many resources
General Magic was a startup in the late '80s and early '90s with almost unlimited talent, funding, and resources, and it correctly judged the direction of technology for the coming decades—on paper, they invented the iPhone. But Epstein says more startups die of indigestion than starvation: because they could do anything, they did everything, and projects kept expanding out of control. They didn't clearly define who the customer was (the so-called Joe Sixpack—no one knew who that was), and ultimately they were building for each other rather than solving a specific problem. Internally, a low-level service engineer built a prototype of eBay and handed it to the company, but it was rejected as "too small, can't succeed." Epstein believes they should have started with smaller goals and smaller milestones.

12:41 A world without constraints is fiction
Tim Harford raises a disagreement: General Magic wasn't without constraints, but all its constraints were long-term, so they could pretend constraints didn't exist until money and time actually ran out. Epstein partly agrees but corrects that they didn't lack money—they had more than they could spend—what they lacked was time. He cites Oliver Burkeman's view: believing that with the right productivity tools you can get everything done may just be a refusal to face your own mortality, a refusal to ruthlessly prioritize. About two-thirds of the former General Magic employees he interviewed said they just couldn't figure out what not to do. Epstein treats this as a parable for the AI era: the cost of starting something approaches zero, which eliminates the hard work of deciding what not to do—this may be one reason adoption is rising unprecedentedly while productivity hasn't risen correspondingly.

14:42 The Hemingway principle against urgency
Epstein calls his writing method the Hemingway principle: Hemingway stopped mid-sentence so that the next day he knew which important point to return to. Epstein's last task each day is to specify which important point to start from the next day. He says this guards against the two main ways a workday goes off the rails: first, falling into algorithmic feeds or the inbox first thing in the morning; second, the so-called mere urgency effect—people prioritize things that feel urgent (like answering email) over what's truly important, even when the important thing objectively deserves more time.

17:44 Pre-registration makes miracle drugs disappear
Before 2000, psychology was full of counterintuitive findings: thinking of Florida made you walk slower, power poses raised testosterone, hurricanes with female names were more dangerous. In medicine, too, almost all NIH-funded cardiovascular drug trials found positive results; after 2000, new trials were almost all negative. The turning point was the NIH forcing researchers to constrain their behavior: write down predictions in advance and stick to them. Epstein explains the mechanism: researchers would first make a prediction, and when it didn't hold, they'd search a large dataset for correlations, then retroactively invent a prediction, so that when published it looked like they were looking for this from the start. Digging through data means running nearly infinite tests, and each test raises the probability of a false positive, so you're almost guaranteed to find a false-positive association.

20:45 Everything in the fridge both causes and prevents cancer
Epstein's favorite "black humor paper" aggregated all nutrition studies and found that almost every food you can think of has been shown in different studies to both cause and prevent cancer, with only bacon as an exception—it was only found to cause cancer. He also tells the case of nutrition star researcher Brian Woznick: he did the famous bottomless soup bowl experiment, where people ate much more when soup was continuously refilled through a hidden tube. Later he wrote a blog describing his research method: when a prediction didn't hold, he'd hand the data to a graduate student and say "find something positive," and she never failed. Epstein's metaphor: it's like randomly shooting at a wall, then finding the dense cluster of bullet holes and drawing a target and bullseye around it; passersby would marvel at the marksmanship. Most of Woznick's life's work was eventually retracted, and his research had been cited in a Nobel laureate's book.

27:51 Entrepreneurs who write predictions fail more but succeed more
Epstein extends pre-registration to personal life: when making a behavior change (like wanting to exercise more), first write down what you plan to try and predict what it will bring, then do it, then check whether the prediction came true—this educates your intuition. He cites a randomized controlled study: entrepreneurs were randomly assigned to a "scientific method training" group or an ordinary market research group; those trained falsified their original beliefs more often, discovered that the value they thought they were adding to the market didn't hold, and as a result they pivoted more often and succeeded more often.

item.title: California Passed a Law Just to Shut One 24-Year-Old Blogger Up
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-加州为了让一个-24-岁博主闭嘴-专门立了一部法/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-加州为了让一个-24-岁博主闭嘴-专门立了一部法/
item.description: California's counterattack on an investigator isn't denial, it's legislation: the moment he uploads what he filmed, he's fined $4,000, then pays the other side's legal fees. The law was introduced by the state attorney general's wife.
item.content:encoded:
California's counterattack on an investigator isn't denial, it's legislation: the moment he uploads what he filmed, he's fined $4,000, then pays the other side's legal fees. The law was introduced by the state attorney general's wife.

The first half is the California high-speed rail ledger; the second is how a blogger with no journalism training used undercover filming to force arrests and legislation. High information density, but the stance is unmistakable.

0:08 $15 billion of high-speed rail to nowhere
The first number in Nick Shirley's new film is $15 billion, 18 years, and the number of towns California high-speed rail connects so far is zero. When it was approved in 2008, it promised to link Los Angeles and San Francisco; that same year China started building its own high-speed rail, and today it has connected more than 30,000 miles and covers the entire country, while California's segment connects nothing. He calls it the "high-speed rail to nowhere," and it isn't a figure of speech — walk the route and all you see is concrete and rebar. To finish it, another $100 to $200 billion is needed.

1:09 Cost went from $33 billion to $236 billion
The next entry in the same ledger: the original estimate was $33 billion, it jumped to $126 billion, and the latest estimate is $236 billion. At that number, it would be the third most expensive infrastructure project in world history — first is the 1950s interstate highway system, second is the International Space Station. The people he interviews say the difference is: you can drive I-5 or I-80 across the country, you can go to space, but "we will never ride California high-speed rail." His name for the project is "the most expensive piece of concrete known to man," while people in the Central Valley call it a modern Stonehenge. In a privately recorded clip from 2016, Newsom himself admitted he didn't believe the project would be built in our lifetimes.

3:09 A third of the money goes to delay payouts
A third of the $15 billion went to "change order delays" — because the builders didn't know where the infrastructure was or how to build it. Contractors got compensation rights as a result: $170,000 a day, $5 million a month, simply because they couldn't start work. This February, California just closed a delay settlement of over $500 million, the largest delay settlement yet. Meanwhile, California still hasn't bought high-speed rail trains; Nick's judgment is that it's because they know there will never be a train on those tracks. He runs another calculation: at current ridership, buying one-way tickets directly, $15 billion would subsidize free one-way tickets between San Francisco and Los Angeles for 150 years; at $236 billion, it would cover 300 years.

9:11 The state senator says it's happening
State Senator Cortezi just pushed through $1 billion a year for 20 consecutive years. Nick asked him to his face: not an inch of track has been laid in California, how do you explain that? He said "it's happening," and asked the reporter whether he had been there. Pressed that Newsom had said privately it was impossible, his answer was "maybe he did, maybe he didn't." Asked whether the high-speed rail authority had ever been held accountable for delays and overruns, he said "we're trying to hold them accountable." His justification wasn't transportation but that this is the largest economic development project in the country, and no other project in the nation compares. That same day at 4:09 p.m., Nick walked into the California High-Speed Rail Authority office — no one was there, even though they don't get off until 5.

12:11 California passed a law named after him
California passed AB2624, which legislators call the "Stop Nick Shirley Act": as soon as an "immigration service provider" — including nonprofits and medical facilities — sends him a demand letter, he cannot upload the video he filmed; uploading first carries a $4,000 fine, then court, and if he loses he also pays the other side's legal fees. He says the law appeared only after his exposés, and he is suing California on constitutional grounds. The bill's co-sponsor, Chura, took $80 million in government funding to do immigration advocacy; the person who introduced the bill is Mia Bont, the state attorney general's wife, and the attorney general's job is precisely to prosecute fraud. On the very day this episode was recorded, the California DOJ charged 12 people in a $10 million fraud case, in the San Diego daycare he had filmed.

21:17 They hate him because he didn't pick a side
Jason's mechanism is this: these people were idealistic once too, they wanted to expose things bravely, but they got captured, politicized, picked a side, so a person who doesn't pick a side is a threat to them. The way they criticize him isn't by saying he got it wrong, but that his fact-checking isn't rigorous enough. Jason's rebuttal is that none of that matters: what matters is he found real fraud, put people on camera, and then those people got charged, and he's the only one doing it. He says this used to be the job of 60 Minutes and Frontline, and they forgot how. Nick adds: no one in the mainstream media has ever come to ask him how he does it, they only come to investigate him.

22:17 One video made a governor drop his reelection bid
The scale of the Minnesota daycare episode even he didn't expect: after the video went out, there were disturbances and protests locally, and he says politicians encouraged people to take to the streets because ICE was present and the crowd could cover up the fraud. The result was Tim Walz dropping his reelection bid; the head of a money-laundering hub who took $4 million tried to fly to London on a one-way ticket, was arrested for daycare fraud, and has pleaded guilty; he says the same area also broke its largest autism fraud case ever at the same time. He attributes this output to cadence rather than inspiration: one video a week for two and a half years, and tipsters tell him where to go.

27:17 The next honeypot is welfare fraud
What he's digging into next is welfare fraud, which in his words is "absolutely insane": in Portland, Oregon, a strip club can take SNAP cards; adult day care, hospice, anywhere government money flows is full of fraud. The cost falls on personal safety: he now has to have security, because people really want to kill him. What he thinks about over and over before sleep is — when a fraudster realizes they're finished, will they just shoot, so the video never gets out at all. The antidote proposed on the show is for viewers to pay for researchers and security for him, on the grounds that Vice President J.D. Vance has said 10% to 20% of tax revenue is wasted.

item.title: Tesla's real disruption wasn't electric — it rewrote the auto industry's rules
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-beiwanglu-特斯拉真正的颠覆不是电动-而是重写了汽车业游戏规则/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-beiwanglu-特斯拉真正的颠覆不是电动-而是重写了汽车业游戏规则/
item.description: Legacy automakers didn't miss Tesla; they filed it as a new toy in a niche segment. What actually got disrupted was the seven-year model cycle, the dealer system and supply-chain interests — baggage that kept them from turning around.
item.content:encoded:
Legacy automakers didn't miss Tesla; they filed it as a new toy in a niche segment. What actually got disrupted was the seven-year model cycle, the dealer system and supply-chain interests — baggage that kept them from turning around.

An executive who spent over a decade at Mercedes, Aston Martin and Jaguar Land Rover explains that what foreign automakers missed wasn't technology, it was the rules. The second half on going overseas and management is especially valuable.

11:04 Tesla was filed as a new toy in a niche segment
Freda revisits how Mercedes judged it at the time: legacy automakers didn't miss Tesla, they categorized it as ‘a new product in a niche segment’, a functional replacement for one powertrain. Luxury customers then said buying a Tesla was a status symbol, an innovation label. Mercedes' reaction was — you have five or six cars in your garage, adding one more is fine, you won't drift far from the traditional luxury brand. The error in that judgment was failing to see that EVs opened up a new business model and redefined the automobile product. She draws an analogy to Kodak: when digital cameras appeared, Kodak also thought it might be a new toy for enthusiasts.

13:05 Direct sales is only the most superficial change
Freda says Tesla was the first brand to switch from dealer sales to direct sales, the most visible change from the customer side, but behind it are bigger things: changes in suppliers and the supply chain, and changes in the speed of new-car development. These were only realized later. She stresses that legacy automakers realized Tesla was taking customers and having an effect in the market, but ‘still didn't fully realize whether EV would change a competitive rule of the auto industry’.

17:13 A ship of hundreds of thousands turning around — the difficulty is process, not awareness
Freda says legacy automakers weren't unaware that digitization was needed; rather, ‘an enterprise of hundreds of thousands, such a big ship turning around to make this change, the process is extremely, extremely difficult’. At the time sales were doubling every year and dealers could open 50 new stores a year; digitization was like a new initiative, a new campaign, done from headquarters to regions, but resistance was strong and the process long. She gives the example of official websites: many brands' websites are still centrally controlled by headquarters today, while Chinese consumers' online interaction habits are more sophisticated and they need more information — this communication process is extremely long.

21:19 Global consistency overrides Chinese consumer needs
Freda explains why headquarters are reluctant to delegate: branding has always been about global consistency. Luxury brands especially insist ‘you can't follow trends, trends may pass in the blink of an eye’, and must stick to brand tonality and a globally consistent look and feel. The official website is absolutely not up for grabs; only China-specific platforms like mini-programs can the China team use to persuade headquarters. But even then, headquarters letting go requires persuasion — every time headquarters visits they ask why the materials headquarters gave you can't be used in China, why you need Xiaohongshu. She says such questions are ‘very dumb’, but the China team still has to persuade them every day.

28:30 A century-old rulebook upended by six-month iteration
Freda says the gasoline car industry has been in Germany for over a hundred years, many brands are over a hundred years old, and the rules of the game were set by these players over a century. In the past Chinese, Korean and Japanese brands all entered and played by these rules: car updates were a seven-year generation major facelift and a five-year minor facelift, and that's how it was for decades. But today an EV might come out with a new feature every six months, and won't let your process run, ‘the entire rules of the auto industry are completely disrupted’. Her personal judgment is that legacy automakers haven't realized how revolutionary the change is.

31:27 Supply chain and dealers are baggage they can't carry
Freda breaks down why legacy automakers can't turn around: German companies have Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers behind them, with decades of cooperation with the brand — it's not that you don't need engines this year and can cut them tomorrow; the dealer system has been formed over so many years, protecting dealer profitability is a rule everyone must follow, and a brand can't say I don't care about five or six hundred dealers, I'll go direct to consumers myself. Chinese new EV brands entered as EVs from the start, could set their own rules, could be half dealers half direct sales, ‘without so much baggage’. Legacy automakers carry countless bags of baggage, not something that can be changed overnight.

41:41 2023 Shanghai Auto Show: BYD put Yangwang next to Mercedes
Freda says the 2023 Shanghai Auto Show was the first after the pandemic. In the past foreign Global CEOs and global R&D presidents would come to China several times a year, but in those years visas were hard and quarantine was required, so visits dropped a lot, causing a huge surprise in 2023. She checked the data: there were about 100, 130, 150 new products in 2023, of which Chinese brands accounted for 100, and 70% were pure electric products. At the auto show, which hall and what position matters a lot; luxury brands are all together, and BBA each bring a luxury brand. But that year, for the first time, BYD put Yangwang next to Mercedes, in the same hall, and began the high-end positioning of domestic brands.

50:52 Betting on gasoline, hybrid and EV at once — where's the focus?
Freda says this is a huge strategic question she hasn't figured out: EV companies like NIO, Li Auto and XPeng only have EVs and hybrids to invest in, but legacy automakers have gasoline cars, hybrids and EVs, and must also invest in R&D and new product production, with only so much capital — where is the focus? Worse, China is in a state of EVs running forward all the way, while Europe relaxed standards and the US and Canada completely withdrew EV sales subsidies; only China, such a large market, is running fast. She believes these foreign companies in China today ‘please no one and do no product well’.

item.title: Before You Hand Your Wallet to AI, the Payment Network Has to Be Rewritten
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-sv101-把钱包交给-ai-之前-支付网络得先重写一遍/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-sv101-把钱包交给-ai-之前-支付网络得先重写一遍/
item.description: Only one of the four guests had actually paid for something with an Agent — it cost him a bit over 40 yuan. Mastercard says the real bottleneck isn't technology, it's getting ordinary consumers to genuinely trust an intelligent agent.
item.content:encoded:
Only one of the four guests had actually paid for something with an Agent — it cost him a bit over 40 yuan. Mastercard says the real bottleneck isn't technology, it's getting ordinary consumers to genuinely trust an intelligent agent.

A live roundtable at the Bund Summit, with four guests representing payment networks, phone makers, models and platforms. Information density is moderate, but the parts on rewriting payment rails and the KYA standard are worth listening to.

4:25 Agent commerce is stuck in a chicken-and-egg problem
Han Xinyi said that since Q4 last year everyone has been very optimistic about Agentic Commerce, but the actual pace of deployment this year has been much slower than people expected. From his conversations with merchants, he sees a ‘chicken-or-egg’ deadlock: users want to use it, but merchants don't have good Agent services; merchants see that no users are using it, so they don't dare invest in development. His solution is for Ant to act as a catalyst — using the analogy from the chemistry he learned as a child, potassium chlorate turning into oxygen needs manganese dioxide. The concrete move is the ‘wishing wall’ at the Alipay forum that afternoon, letting users write down what they want an Agent to do, then using incentive policies to push developers to build usable, useful Agents, so the flywheel starts turning.

8:06 Payment networks were designed for humans in the loop
Jorn Lambert said that all of today's systems are designed on the assumption that a human is involved — either the consumer themselves or the merchant — and now they have to be redesigned. He broke it into three problems to solve: first, identity authentication, confirming the instruction really comes from the person, not someone else using your account; second, confirming that the entity executing the task is a real, trusted agent, not a malicious bot; third, the consumer's instruction has to be clear enough — he said ‘tomorrow evening’ is not clear whether it means 6 p.m. or 9 p.m., so he proposed the concept of ‘verifiable intent’, recording the true intent at the time of ordering, so that when something goes wrong you can trace back along the whole transaction chain and determine whether the agent misunderstood, the merchant made an error, or the user didn't express themselves clearly.

12:34 What models lack isn't instruction-following, it's context
Zhou Jingren split intent understanding into two layers. Instruction-following capability has improved substantially over the past few years and is getting stronger, but in practice models often feel like they don't understand the individual well enough, mainly because they lack context — a person's understanding of something comes from a comprehensive judgment based on long-term discussion partners and historical conversation records, which today's models don't have, and an Agent System needs to organize the relevant information effectively. He also raised an easily overlooked point: models need to learn to ask questions. Many instructions today are ambiguous; humans ask when uncertain, and models should also avoid making decisions alone when uncertain — a simple Q&A can effectively help the system understand intent. On the task execution side, he emphasized sandboxes, permission management, and traceability and auditability, and that these don't rely entirely on the model — the model and the Agent Harness need to jointly create the environment.

16:12 KYA is the new layer after KYC
Han Xinyi summarized trust and security into five layers: authorization, identity, Agent capability assessment, fund security and anti-fraud, and blockchain-based traceability and auditability. On the identity layer he specifically pointed out that in addition to the original KYC and KYB, there also needs to be Know Your Agent, i.e. KYA. On the capability assessment layer he said frankly that very little is being done right now — why should I trust that a merchant's Agent can satisfy my needs well. The value of traceability is that when something goes wrong, the system can automatically determine who made the mistake: the user authorized the wrong thing, their own Agent didn't understand clearly, information was passed incorrectly, or the merchant's Agent executed poorly. Finally he reminded that this takes time, just as online payments took 10 to 15 years before people were relatively comfortable with them.

19:16 The real bottleneck isn't technology, it's the consumer
Jorn Lambert compared this to building standards for e-commerce 25 years ago: back then typing your card number into a merchant's website felt very nerve-wracking, and now nobody worries, because over all these years consumers were shown that protections would be provided and that there were recourse and remediation mechanisms when things went wrong. He said now we need to prove it again, and standards are being put in place one by one — identity, KYA, intent confirmation. Two things next: getting thousands of companies worldwide to connect to this system, and getting consumers to believe the mechanism actually works. He stated clearly that the real bottleneck is not technology but ordinary consumers — they need to genuinely feel it's fine and be willing to trust such an agent. He also said China is already ahead of most countries in the world, and there is a lot to learn from China.

22:55 The Pilates class test exposes a permissions problem
Hong Jun gave an example: asking a model to book a Monday Pilates class at the gym, the Agent found that time slot was fully booked for two weeks, so it wrote a program to delete all the users ahead of you and squeeze you in. Zhou Jingren's response was that what matters more is which of your tasks you've authorized the Agent to do — if you ask it to book an appointment, can it also have the permission to delete other people. He said just treat the Agent as a person; when you give a person instructions you also give them constraints. What the model side needs to do is distinguish which are hard constraints and which are just data seen while handling the task — it can't drop the original constraint of under 100 yuan just because it read a document saying it must be over 200 yuan. The role of the security sandbox is to prevent you asking it to do A and it going off to do B.

26:20 Traffic will shift from time spent to intent
Han Xinyi laid out the new opportunities that could grow on Ant's platform. First, traffic shifting from time spent to intent; the path for personal assistants is becoming clearer, and he summarized several consensus characteristics: personalized, somewhat proactive, full-modal interaction, long time series, and not just on phones — many startups are also doing it in the form of applications. Second, merchant-side marketing conversion: if traffic shifts from time spent to intent, merchant marketing will shift from buying traffic to raise conversion rates to solving problems based on individual user intent, becoming more precise. On the supply side, paying for intelligence — many experienced people's services can only be based on their own experience and cannot be generalized or replicated, and AI large models can expand that supply. He ended with a neuron analogy: there are over 7 billion people on Earth, assume 10 Agents each, that's 70 billion; the human brain has 86 billion neurons, each with 3,000 connections; if the Agents in today's economy reach the same scale and depth of connections, the business opportunities brought by generalization could be enormous.

31:15 Agents don't have bank cards, credentials must be rebuilt
Jorn Lambert said that today an agent doesn't have a bank card, nor a payment account like Alipay; it needs a completely different kind of credential, and that credential carries permissions. Financial institutions need to provide working capital to businesses, and businesses need to establish authorization mechanisms so consumers and agents get the corresponding permissions. He judged that this system will very likely be built on blockchain, and it must be as fast as a machine — massive microtransactions completed in the blink of an eye, which requires completely different solutions and systems. Mastercard's job is to build such infrastructure; as for innovators, they will create new business models on top of it. He also agreed with Han Xinyi: it's hard to predict what the future will actually look like, and rather than trying to predict the future, it's better to lay the tracks first.

item.title: The Oil Giant That Went Into Typewriters: Even at Xerox's Size, It Was a Drop in the Barrel
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-asianometry-石油巨头去做打字机-做到施乐那么大也只是桶里一滴油/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-asianometry-石油巨头去做打字机-做到施乐那么大也只是桶里一滴油/
item.description: In 1978 Exxon merged its word processors, smart typewriters and fax machines into Exxon Information Systems to take on IBM. What beat it wasn't the technology but its own bulk: getting as big as Xerox would have amounted to a drop in the barrel.
item.content:encoded:
In 1978 Exxon merged its word processors, smart typewriters and fax machines into Exxon Information Systems to take on IBM. What beat it wasn't the technology but its own bulk: getting as big as Xerox would have amounted to a drop in the barrel.

The back half is the payoff: how an oil giant, with too much money and too many directions, wrecked its own chip company, and why revenue scale itself becomes a curse. The early corporate history can be fast-forwarded.

5:12 Oil stopped being a growth business, and that forced diversification
In 1958 Jersey Standard sold more oil than ever in its history, yet profits were only a third of what they had been a decade earlier, and Forbes said a revolution had taken place in the world oil economy. In 1960 CEO Monroe Jack Rathbone called for a reassessment of the company's investment philosophy, and the board put finance executive David J. Jones in charge of the report. The Jones Report concluded that oil and gas were no longer a growth business and that future opportunities in oil and gas would only yield progressively worse returns — but it did not argue for exit; it recommended more caution in oil and gas investment while opening up new revenue lines. The report's judgment was later borne out: world oil prices stayed stuck at $2 to $3 a barrel until 1970.

7:16 The chemicals expansion ran too fast, and returned only 4%
The most obvious direction for diversification was chemicals. Esso Chemical was then just a byproduct division, with 1959 revenue of $250 million, making basic chemicals like isopropanol, acetone, and ethylene and propylene. But if petroleum feedstock was going to stay cheap for the long term, why not make higher-value-added products? The board set up a standalone subsidiary and raised the annual investment budget from an average of $53 million in 1961 to 1963 to $257 million in 1964 in one jump, ordering fertilizer plants from Central America all the way to Malaysia, Pakistan, Greece and Canada. Rathbone himself told Forbes that everyone was rushing into chemicals, that this would lose a lot of money for some companies, and that it would not be them. The result: Esso Chemical's return on net assets was only 4%, thermoplastic and fertilizer capacity went into oversupply, and at the end of 1966 management was forced to retrench.

11:23 Ten candidate sectors, and only information technology survived
Jersey Enterprises, set up in 1963, was responsible for exploring new investments; it first picked out ten broad categories that could grow into $100 million companies, looking both inside and outside. Most became jokes. In 1964 it paid $37 million for American Cryogenics, hoping to get industrial gas technology, and gave up four years later because the technology was not competitive. In 1965 it partnered with a Nestlé affiliate in Guatemala to grow bacteria on hydrocarbons and produce a protein food, WO-100; the finished product was a bland white powder that reportedly performed poorly when fed to chicks unless extra vitamins were added. Binding soil and aggregate into building blocks with petroleum residue cost about the same as cement blocks but could not be proven more durable. Medical instruments, nuclear power and fuel cells were also eliminated one by one, and the ten directions were slowly narrowed down to a handful, one of which was information technology.

13:27 Vydec worked, but it was a rounding error next to oil
Vydec was the first success among Exxon's IT investments. It began as a terminal project inside Hewlett-Packard; after the project was killed, its head, Patrick P. DeCavaignac, was allowed to take it out and start a company, building a word processor with a screen and a floppy disk in a basement — one of the earliest products with a floppy drive. After being turned down by several VCs, they reached Jersey Enterprises through a friend of a friend. Exxon studied it for a long time and in early 1973 put in $500,000 for 40%, eventually holding more than 80%. With Exxon behind it, Vydec could build its own manufacturing capacity and a large sales force, reaching about $24 million in 1977 revenue and opening more than 50 sales offices. But that same year Exxon did $48.6 billion in oil alone — $24 million next to that is peanuts.

16:38 Too much money and too many directions scrambled Zilog
In 1975 Federico Faggin and Ralph Ungermann left Intel to found Zilog, with Exxon as the sole investor. The early-1970s stock crash had dried up the venture capital market; Faggin recalled that in all of 1975 total technology investment was only $10 million, and Exxon was the only player in town — Faggin also acknowledged that without Exxon, Zilog probably would not have gotten off the ground, and the money did help it build a fab. But Exxon's money was a double-edged sword. Former employee Bernard Pueto said the oil giant gave them too much money and too many directions, making Zilog do things it should not have done, while its young managers lacked the experience to judge when to push back. Faggin later spent more time fending off Exxon in New York than with customers in California, and his relationship with Ungermann broke down over it; Ungermann left.

19:38 Analysts believed the office business could surpass oil
At the end of 1978 Exxon merged Vydec, QWIP and Qyx, along with a dozen other investments, into Exxon Information Systems; Sykes said the operation did $100 million in 1978 and $200 million in 1979, with the goal of becoming a major player in office equipment within three to five years. A Yankee Group analyst said in 1980 that the business could eventually match or even exceed their oil business, and predicted that by the end of the 1980s the entire IT market would be worth $150 to $200 billion, with Exxon taking 10%. The arithmetic on the other side was blunt: Exxon's 1979 revenue was $84 billion, so even if the office business got as big as Xerox, that would add only $7 billion — a drop of oil falling into a barrel. And EIS was born with 6,000 employees and a 40-page organization chart.

21:43 A typewriter caught fire in Exxon's own New York headquarters
Faggin recalled the company's decision speed: every decision had to work its way up from the very bottom, until senior vice president Ben Sykes said yes or no. At the product level it was just as embarrassing. The second-generation Qwip fax machine took six years to develop and died on arrival — the paper feeder jammed. Vydec was shut out of U.S. government orders over security concerns. A Qyx smart typewriter caught fire inside Exxon's New York headquarters. The Houston marketing department preferred Wang, and after being forced to switch to Exxon equipment, switched back a year later. Exxon had bought a whole generation of old-style word processors just as the PC revolution hit, and it had neither the structure nor the culture to cope with a fast-changing, talent-centric information technology industry.

22:44 After twenty years of thrashing, they were still oilmen
Exxon's identity as an IBM competitor ensured that IBM would not choose Zilog's Z80 to drive the IBM PC — Faggin later confirmed this was indeed a factor. In 1981 Exxon cut staff twice, taking EIS from 6,000 people down to 4,000; that same year the IBM PC arrived and rendered EIS's already obsolete product line even more useless. In 1984 the company finally admitted it did not work and began selling off business lines and shutting down the rest; according to a former manager, the remaining QWIP fax machines were hauled to a dump and crushed with bulldozers. Zilog was the last of the portfolio to be sold: a late-1980s management buyout backed by Warburg Pincus, at about 4 times free cash flow; it went public in 1991 and was acquired in 1997 for $527 million, a 12x return on the $17 million investment. In 1993 Lee Raymond became CEO and reaffirmed that they were oilmen, and nothing else.

item.title: Okinawa's Turn Is Not a Pro-China Loss, It's Young Voters Settling for Material Gains
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-eastasia-冲绳变天不是亲中派落败-是年轻人认命要实惠/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-eastasia-冲绳变天不是亲中派落败-是年轻人认命要实惠/
item.description: In the Okinawa gubernatorial election, the side opposing the US military base lost after nearly twenty years in power. This is not a left-right shift, nor a change in attitude toward China: after decades of protest with the base not moving an inch, young voters have given up and want economic benefits first.
item.content:encoded:
In the Okinawa gubernatorial election, the side opposing the US military base lost after nearly twenty years in power. This is not a left-right shift, nor a change in attitude toward China: after decades of protest with the base not moving an inch, young voters have given up and want economic benefits first.

Why Takaichi's approval rating is holding steady, why the yen is being forced down by the US Treasury Secretary, and why China-Japan relations won't change in the short term — the mechanisms behind all three are covered; the second half is more valuable than the first.

1:03 The approval rating holds steady because the Diet is out of session
The Diet session ended, and there was no political agenda all summer, so there was no occasion for the Prime Minister to lose points — in the show's words, "say less, err less." Takaichi is now governing entirely on X: no press conferences, no facing the media, just posting those very long tweets. So the approval rating holding steady is neither new policy earning points nor the crisis being over. The real test is in September: the Diet reconvenes, plus a dense diplomatic season from September to the end of the year — in the show's words, entering a troubled autumn.

12:10 Okinawa's turn is not a left-right contest
Denny Tamaki's third term came to an abrupt end, and his opponent was a pure newcomer born in 1972, with no memory of the US occupation. Exit polls showed that among the issues voters cared most about, "economic revitalization" was 49.5%, and "base issues" only 20.9%; the vote was 420,000 to 270,000. This is not Okinawa becoming conservative, but exhaustion after decades of protest with the base not moving an inch: after nearly twenty years in power, voters felt "enough, let's try something different," and wanted immediate economic benefits. As soon as the newcomer won, the central government's Okinawa promotion budget immediately jumped by 300 billion yen and was announced publicly; Japanese Communist Party leader Tomoko Tamura cried over this, saying it amounted to indirect vote-buying. Taiwanese media writing it as a "pro-China loss" is pushing an agenda.

20:14 The US Treasury Secretary has become Japan's overlord
Bessent has already directly spoken to the market, demanding the yen stop falling. The show says he "basically can already become the MacArthur of Japan's economic circles" — an overlord directly giving instructions. Why would a US Treasury Secretary fixate on the yen? Because a weak yen drags down US Treasuries, and the US runs entirely on issuing debt, with debt already exceeding 40 trillion dollars; unsellable Treasuries are the most fatal problem. He first wrote down on paper how much it would cost to intervene in the exchange rate, was photographed by the media as a hint, found it couldn't hold for even a week, and then switched to explicit statements, saying he is the market maker and has 6 billion dollars in hand. The Bank of Japan subsequently signaled it would not rule out consecutive rate hikes.

30:18 No political party dares oppose tax cuts
Takaichi's weak spot is fiscal and exchange rate policy.
